docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Companion wiki · Manuscript V3

This wiki is a browsable, living companion to the review Self-Driving Laboratories for Formulation: Handling Liquids, Pastes, Powders and Objects, from Robots to Digital Twins and AI Agents. It follows the review's seven steps and includes its tables, all ten figures and 178 linked references.

Formulation means combining ingredients into products whose properties depend on both composition and process. An autonomous formulation experiment is a physical choreography:

  1. ingredients with very different rheology are dosed into one premix container;
  2. the container is carried to a mixer;
  3. the mix is processed and characterized, often with materials the robot has never handled.

Landmark SDLs show that this physical layer can limit autonomy as much as the planning algorithm does [3], [4]. The guiding question at every step is how should this material, in this container, be handled next?

Liquids Semi-solids Powders Objects

Graphical abstract.

docs.title: Self-Driving Laboratories for Formulation
docs.text:
How a self-driving lab doses liquids, pastes and powders, moves the containers that hold them, rehearses each step in a digital twin, and decides what to make next.

Open the atlas Seven-step map Figures

docs.title: The seven steps
docs.text:
1 Dose How is each ingredient dosed? Materials, dispensing, 20 scenarios, strategies

2 Move How do containers move? Gantries, SCARA, arms, cobots, mobile manipulators

3 Buy What can be bought? Dispensers and integrated platforms by accuracy and price

4 Extend How to go beyond the catalog? Retrofits: end-effectors, sensors, control software

5 Rehearse Will the plan work? Fidelity hierarchy, simulators, digital twins

6 Orchestrate How do devices run as one? Layers L1–L4, interfaces, eight open-source systems

7 Decide What to make next? Data, surrogates, Bayesian optimization, AI agents

docs.text:

  • Figures are shown as cards. Admonitions use the site palette.

docs.title: 2026-11-07: Rebuilt and updated to manuscript V3
docs.text:
The wiki was rebuilt as part of the formulation-sdl-atlas repository. It was updated to the final V3 manuscript, Self-Driving Laboratories for Formulation: Handling Liquids, Pastes, Powders and Objects, from Robots to Digital Twins and AI Agents (Rastegardoost, Bao, Sadr, Abdollahi, Darvish, Clasky, Ohsaka, Le Devedec; manuscript in preparation, 2026).

The earlier wiki was published at https://accelerationconsortium.github.io/material-handling/ and was written from an older draft. Its pages were reconstructed from the published site and kept in the same navigation groups.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: We welcome contributions from the community to keep this wiki accurate and up to date.

docs.title: Ways to Contribute
docs.text:
• Fix errors or outdated information
  • Add missing technologies or references
  • Improve clarity of existing pages
  • Add new subsections for emerging methods

docs.title: How to Contribute
docs.text:
1. Click the Edit this page button (pencil icon, top right of any page).
  2. This opens the file on GitHub. Sign in and click Fork this repository.
  3. Make your changes in the Markdown file.
  4. Submit a Pull Request with a brief description of what you changed and why.

docs.title: Content Guidelines
docs.text:
• Keep descriptions concise and factual.
  • Cite primary sources (journal articles, manufacturer documentation). Numbered citations such as [11] refer to the review's reference list on the References page; link them as [\[11\]](references.md#ref-11).
  • Accuracy and price figures should match the review (V3) or state their own source and date.
  • Use the existing page structure (Overview → Technologies → Comparison → References).
  • Avoid promotional language.

docs.title: Local Development
docs.text:
To preview the site locally before submitting:

pip install mkdocs-material
cd wiki-src
mkdocs serve

The built site is published from the wiki/ folder of the repository (mkdocs build --site-dir ../wiki).

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
All ten figures of the review (the graphical abstract and Figures 1–9) appear here with their full captions. Click any image to enlarge it. Under each caption are links to the wiki pages that discuss that figure. Numbers in square brackets link to the References.

Graphical abstract

The seven steps of a formulation SDL at a glance: dose, move, buy, extend, rehearse, orchestrate and decide.

Discussed in: Home

Figure 1

A formulation SDL and its digital twin. Physical cell (left): a CNC gantry with dispenser rack and balance (1–3), a SCARA elevator serving two characterizers (4–6) and an arm loading the mixer (7, 8). Digital twin (right): robot trajectories (A), material models (B), virtual sensors (C) and GPU simulation (D) rehearse each step before it runs.

Discussed in: Seven-step map

Figure 2

Material properties and handling mechanisms: (A) liquids to pastes and (B) powders by cohesion; (C, E, G) selection charts and (D, F, H) mechanisms for liquids, semi-solids and powders. Product photographs adapted from Opentrons [15], Hamilton [16], Nordson EFD [17] and XQ Instruments; powder dispensers are compared in [18].

Discussed in: Material Properties · Dispensing by Material Class

Figure 3

Literature scenarios titled by their sense–act sequence and adapted from the cited studies: liquids (A–H) [11], [22], [23], [24], [25], [26], [27], [28], semi-solids (I–L) [31], [32], [33], [34] and powders and granular media (M–T) [12], [37], [38], [39], [40], [41], [42], [43].

Discussed in: Literature Scenarios

Figure 4

Robot classes for object handling, ordered by axes, reach and cost: (A) Cartesian gantry, (B) SCARA, (C) 6-DOF arm, (D) 7-DOF or dual-arm cobot and (E) mobile manipulator; (F) repeatability versus price (Table 2).

Discussed in: Robot Classes

Figure 5

(A) Commercial dispensers and platforms by material class, mechanism and price (hollow markers: quote only; bracketed numbers: references). (B–E) Qualitative 0–10 profiles of four platforms (‘solid handling’: labware transfer). Photographs adapted from Opentrons [15], Chemspeed [71], Hamilton [16] and Eppendorf [75].

Discussed in: Commercial Dispensers · Integrated Platforms · By Yield Stress & Cost

Figure 6

Four fidelity levels of a formulation twin, (A) workflow, (B) kinematics, (C) contact dynamics and (D) material physics, at rising compute cost, with example tools (SimPy, MoveIt 2, MuJoCo, Isaac Lab; screenshots and logos from the projects’ repositories under MIT, BSD-3-Clause and Apache-2.0 licenses; logos are trademarks of their owners).

Discussed in: Simulation & Digital Twins

Figure 7

The digital twin as a working environment: (A) motion planning in ROS 2 with MoveIt 2, (B) a GPU simulator interface, (C) a DEM/MPM material solver and (D) rehearsal of AI-proposed plans before release to the cell.

Discussed in: Simulation & Digital Twins

Figure 8

Architecture of a formulation SDL: (A) execution and equipment hierarchies, (B) functional layers of orchestration software and (C) functions provided by eight open-source systems (details in Supplementary Table S1).

Discussed in: System Architecture & Orchestration

Figure 9

The decision ladder: data (bottom), models that choose the next experiment (middle) and AI agents (top), connected to the robots by software and data pipelines (right).

Discussed in: Data & Decision Models

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: A reference guide for key terms and concepts in autonomous material handling.

docs.title: Material Properties
docs.text: Yield Stress The minimum stress required to initiate flow in a material. Materials with high yield stress (like pastes and slurries) require more force to move. Rheology The science of material deformation and flow. Describes how materials respond to applied forces and stresses. Viscosity A measure of a fluid's resistance to flow. High viscosity materials (like honey) flow slowly; low viscosity materials (like water) flow easily. Flowability The ease with which a material can be moved, poured, or dispensed. Depends on particle size, shape, moisture content, and cohesion. Non-Newtonian Fluid A fluid whose viscosity changes with the applied shear rate. Examples: ketchup, blood, paint (shear-thinning), or Oobleck (shear-thickening). Cohesion The attractive forces between particles in a powder or semi-solid, affecting how they stick together and flow. Particle Size Distribution (PSD) The range and relative proportions of particle sizes in a powder. Affects flowability and packing density.

docs.title: Handling Strategies
docs.text: Characterize, Then Act A strategy of measuring material properties first, then executing a pre-planned handling procedure based on those measurements. Iterative Optimization A strategy involving repeated cycles of dispense → measure → adjust to optimize process outcomes. Real-Time Correction A strategy that uses in-situ sensors to detect deviations during a process and corrects them on-the-fly. Feedforward Prediction A strategy that predicts the optimal process parameters before execution using prior knowledge or models. Simulation-Based Generalization A strategy of training models in simulation, then deploying them to handle real materials with different properties. Physical Reinvention A strategy of solving handling challenges by redesigning hardware (nozzles, feeders, grippers, etc.). Tactile Retrieval A strategy using touch-based sensing (force, texture, compliance) to manipulate objects without vision.

docs.title: Hardware & Equipment
docs.text: Peristaltic Pump A pump that moves fluid by compressing and releasing a flexible tube in sequence. Good for viscous or particulate fluids. Syringe Pump A pump that dispenses fluid by pushing a plunger through a syringe. Precise but limited volume. Auger / Screw Feeder A rotating screw mechanism for handling powders and granules, providing controlled dispensing rates. Gripper A mechanical or pneumatic device for grasping and manipulating solid objects or partially formed items. Powder Hopper A container that feeds powder into a dispenser or processing unit, often with vibration or agitation. Rheometer An instrument that measures the flow and deformation properties of materials under controlled conditions.

docs.title: AI & Control Concepts
docs.text: Feedback Control A control system that measures output and adjusts input to maintain desired performance (e.g., PID control). Feedforward Control A control system that predicts required adjustments based on known inputs, without measuring output. Cascade Control A hierarchical control structure where an outer controller sets targets for inner controllers. PID Control (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) A standard feedback control algorithm that adjusts output based on error (proportional), accumulated error (integral), and error rate (derivative). Machine Learning (ML) Algorithms that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed. Regression An ML task that predicts continuous numerical values (e.g., predicting dispense volume from parameters). Classification An ML task that predicts categorical outcomes (e.g., predicting material type from sensor data). Digital Twin A virtual model of a physical system that simulates its behavior, used for testing and prediction. Discrete Element Method (DEM) A simulation technique for modeling particle interactions in powders and granular materials. Finite Element Method (FEM) A simulation technique for modeling continuous deformation in solids and semi-solids.

docs.title: Process Metrics
docs.text: Precision The consistency or repeatability of a process. Low variance in repeated measurements or operations. Accuracy How close a measurement or result is to the true value or target. Throughput The volume or mass of material processed per unit time. Yield The percentage of material successfully processed or dispensed without waste or defects. Process Window The range of operating conditions (e.g., temperature, speed, parameters) within which a process works acceptably.

docs.title: Cross-Cutting Terms
docs.text: Autonomous Formulation The automated design and synthesis of materials or products with minimal human intervention, often using feedback loops and optimization. Closed-Loop System A system with sensors that measure outcomes and adjust inputs to maintain control (feedback). Open-Loop System A system that executes pre-planned instructions without measuring or adjusting based on outcomes. Sensor Fusion Combining data from multiple sensors to improve understanding or control of a process. Payload The material being handled or dispensed in a robotic or automated system. Robustness The ability of a system to maintain performance despite variations in materials, conditions, or disturbances. Scalability The ease with which a process or strategy can be adapted to handle different material types, scales, or production rates.

docs.title: Formulation SDL Terms (added with the V3 update)
docs.text: Self-Driving Laboratory (SDL) A laboratory that closes the loop between experiment design, robotic execution and data analysis, using results to select subsequent experiments with little human intervention [1]. Premix container The vessel into which ingredients are dosed before it is carried to a mixer, processed and characterized. See Robot Classes. Object handling Moving the vessels and tools that hold or dispense materials (carrying containers, opening lids, capping, loading instruments), as opposed to material handling, which moves the matter itself. Hausner ratio Ratio of tapped to bulk density of a powder; ~1.00–1.11 indicates free-flowing and >1.4 very cohesive powder (Table 1 of the review). Sense–act sequence The three-verb title of each literature scenario (e.g. dispense → weigh → optimize) describing how a study senses a material and acts on it. See Literature Scenarios. Retrofit A modification of a purchased platform's end-effector, sensing or control software that unlocks a capability its manufacturer never sold. See Retrofits. Digital twin A persistent virtual counterpart of a specific system that shares its geometry, kinematics and device logic and is kept consistent with its measured state [89], [90]. Fidelity level The amount of physics a simulation resolves: (1) workflow, (2) kinematics, (3) contact dynamics, (4) material physics. See Simulation & Digital Twins. DEM / MPM / SPH / CFD Discrete element method (powders), material point method (pastes and gels), smoothed-particle hydrodynamics and computational fluid dynamics (liquids). Sim-to-real gap The performance drop when a model or policy developed in simulation is deployed on hardware; for liquids, gels and powders it is set by the material model [128]. ROS 2 Robot Operating System 2, the middleware through which most research robots, simulators and planners exchange data [96]. SiLA 2 A laboratory standard defining typed device features with discovery, progress notifications and status subscriptions [167]. OPC UA LADS Information models for laboratory and analytical devices built on industrial OPC UA [168]. Orchestration software Software that runs dispensers, robots, instruments and twin as one system, ordering device operations and tracking resources and locations. See Orchestration. Functional layers (L1–L4) Device control (L1), device integration (L2), workflow orchestration (L3) and decision making (L4). Model Context Protocol (MCP) A protocol through which AI agents call tools; increasingly used to expose orchestration functions to agents [171]. Surrogate model A model mapping composition and process parameters to measured properties, used in place of a lookup table. Acquisition function A rule that ranks candidate experiments using a surrogate's predictions and uncertainty, as in active learning and Bayesian optimization [134], [135]. FAIR data Data that are findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable [133]. Agentic system An LLM wrapped in a loop that plans, calls tools, observes results and revises its plan, as in Coscientist and ChemCrow [125], [127]. See LLMs & AI Agents.

docs.title: The Seven Steps of a Formulation SDL
docs.text:
The review looks at formulation from the point of view of a self-driving laboratory and treats building one as a sequence of steps. Each step answers one question that a team building or extending such a laboratory has to settle. The focus throughout is on physical execution and how it couples to sensing, feedback control and experimental planning. By separating fixed automation from systems that adapt their actions to measured material behavior, the review identifies the solutions available today, the capabilities still missing and the trends likely to shape the next generation of formulation SDLs.

Figure 1. A formulation SDL and its digital twin. Physical cell (left): a CNC gantry with dispenser rack and balance (1–3), a SCARA elevator serving two characterizers (4–6) and an arm loading the mixer (7, 8). Digital twin (right): robot trajectories (A), material models (B), virtual sensors (C) and GPU simulation (D) rehearse each step before it runs.

docs.title: Why the physical layer matters
docs.text:
SDLs close the loop between experiment design, robotic execution and data analysis [1]. Flagship platforms have started to deliver on formulation-like problems. A mobile robotic chemist optimized photocatalyst formulations on its own across a human-scale laboratory, running 688 experiments over eight days [3]. The A-Lab targets solid-state synthesis rather than formulation, but it showed that robotic powder dosing and mixing can run unattended at scale [4]. The idea is older than the name: the robot scientist Adam [5], the Chemputer [6] and closed-loop thin-film discovery [7] each joined planning, execution and characterization in their own way.

These successes also show how much execution costs. Burger et al.'s robotic chemist [3] took substantial engineering so that one robot could navigate the laboratory and dispense, degas and sample ten reagents across several workstations. The A-Lab [4] synthesized 41 of 58 targeted compounds. None of its 17 failures was attributed to handling, yet every result depended on powder dosing, mixing and transfer routines engineered in advance for a fixed set of materials and containers. Groups that operate SDLs keep naming hardware integration and adaptive material handling as persistent barriers to autonomy [1], [8].

Decision making has advanced in parallel. Bayesian optimization selects formulations on tight budgets [137], and agents built on large language models have planned and run chemistry on robots [125], [127]. These methods can only act through hardware that doses, moves and measures materials reliably.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text: Step Question Review section Wiki pages 1 · Dose How is each ingredient dosed? 2. Material Handling Properties, Spectrum, Dispensing by class, Literature scenarios, Strategies 2 · Move How do containers move? 3. Object Handling in Formulation SDLs Robot classes 3 · Buy What can be bought? 4. Commercial Handling Solutions and Integrated Platforms Dispensers, Integrated platforms 4 · Extend How to go beyond the catalog? 5. Customizing Platforms Beyond Their Factory Specification Retrofits 5 · Rehearse Will the plan work? 6. Simulation and Digital Twins in SDLs Simulation & digital twins, Tools 6 · Orchestrate How do devices run as one? 7. System Architecture and Orchestration Architecture, Open-source systems 7 · Decide What to make next? 8. Data, Machine Learning, and AI Agents in Formulation SDLs Data & models, AI agents

docs.title: 1 · Dose
docs.text: This step links the properties that govern liquids, semi-solids and powders (viscosity, yield stress, flowability) to the mechanisms used to handle them. It also reviews how recent studies sense, model and correct the dispensing of unfamiliar ingredients. Twenty literature scenarios, each named after its sense–act sequence, show how far past vendor defaults each material class can be pushed.

docs.title: 2 · Move
docs.text: After dosing, the premix becomes an object that has to be moved. Five robot classes carry containers, open lids and load instruments: Cartesian gantries, SCARA robots, 6-DOF arms, 7-DOF or dual-arm cobots and mobile manipulators. The choice depends on the task, not the material.

docs.title: 3 · Buy
docs.text: This step compares commercial dispensers and integrated platforms on accuracy and cost. Price follows mechanism and ecosystem rather than accuracy, and outside liquid handling it is rarely public.

docs.title: 4 · Extend
docs.text: Low-cost retrofits push purchased platforms past their factory specifications. Examples include new end-effectors, sensors mounted through the tool changer and hardware-agnostic control software.

docs.title: 5 · Rehearse
docs.text: Simulation and digital twins let a laboratory rehearse and check a workflow before any material is committed. The review organizes them in a four-level fidelity hierarchy, and a twin can also act as a gate on autonomous actions.

docs.title: 6 · Orchestrate
docs.text: Orchestration software runs the dispensers, robots, instruments and twin as one system. It tracks what is mounted where, which container holds which premix and how much material is left.

docs.title: 7 · Decide
docs.text: Data, surrogate models, acquisition strategies and AI agents choose the next experiment and assist the people who run the laboratory. They connect to the hardware through APIs and data pipelines.

docs.title: Outlook
docs.text:
The review ends with four directions:

  • Shared benchmarks: reference liquids, pastes and powders, plus reference premix-transfer tasks.
  • Open interfaces between planners, software and hardware.
  • Calibrated twins validated against the physical cell.
  • Safeguards that scale with autonomy [129], [130].

See Future Directions.

docs.title: AI Infrastructure for Autonomous Material Handling
AI Infrastructure for Autonomous Material Handling
docs.text:
Updated to manuscript V3

The review places AI at step 7 (Decide), above a stack of hardware, simulation and orchestration. New pages: Data & Decision Models (what an experiment records; surrogates and acquisition), LLMs & AI Agents (agent roles, autonomy levels and safeguards, Table 7), Simulation & Digital Twins and Orchestration (functional layers L1–L4 and interfaces such as SiLA 2, ROS 2 and MCP). The "Integration Architecture" section below is the earlier wiki's view; the review's layered architecture is on the orchestration page.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This section describes the AI and control systems that enable autonomous material handling: sensing, feedback control, machine learning, and digital twins.

docs.title: Why AI Infrastructure Matters
docs.text:
Raw hardware (pumps, motors, grippers) is necessary but not sufficient for autonomous handling. Intelligence comes from:

  1. Sensing: Measuring material properties and process state in real time
  2. Feedback control: Adjusting equipment parameters based on sensor feedback
  3. Machine learning: Generalizing from past experience to new materials
  4. Digital twins: Simulating outcomes before physical execution
  5. LLM agents: Reasoning about complex tasks and adapting plans

These components together create the "intelligence" that allows a robot to handle 1000 different materials without re-tuning per material.

docs.title: The AI Stack for Material Handling
docs.text:
User / Request
       ↓
   LLM Agent (Strategy Selection)
       ↓
Machine Learning Model (Parameter Prediction)
       ↓
Control System (PID loop, real-time correction)
       ↓
Sensors (Feedback: weight, force, pressure, vision)
       ↓
Hardware (Robot, pump, gripper)
       ↓
Material (Liquid, powder, solid)

docs.title: Sensing Layer
docs.text:
Purpose: Gather information about material properties and process state

Sensor types: - Gravimetric (load cell, balance) - Force/torque (F/T sensors) - Pressure (transducers) - Vision (cameras, depth sensors) - Proprioceptive (joint angles, motor current) - Environmental (temperature, humidity)

Sampling rates: 10 Hz – 1 kHz (depending on process speed)

See: Sensing & Characterization

docs.title: Feedback Control Layer
docs.text:
Purpose: Real-time adjustment of equipment parameters to maintain desired outcome

Control strategies: - Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) - Force control - Impedance control - Adaptive control (parameters change based on material)

Typical loop rate: 100 Hz – 1 kHz

See: Feedback Control

docs.title: Machine Learning Layer
docs.text:
Purpose: Learn from past experience; generalize to new materials

ML techniques: - Regression (linear, polynomial, neural networks) - Classification (decision trees, random forests) - Unsupervised (clustering, dimensionality reduction) - Reinforcement learning (trial-and-error policy learning)

Training data required: 20–500 examples (depends on problem complexity)

See: Machine Learning

docs.title: Digital Twins & Simulation
docs.text:
Purpose: Predict outcomes before executing; train models; understand failure modes

Simulator technologies: - Discrete element method (DEM) for powders - Finite element method (FEM) for liquids/gels - Rigid body dynamics for solid handling - Fluid-structure interaction (FSI) for complex flows

See: Digital Twins & LLMs

docs.title: Monolithic Approach (Single Language/Framework)
docs.text: All AI components in one codebase (Python + TensorFlow + ROS): - Pros: Fast integration, unified logging - Cons: Rigid, hard to replace individual components

docs.title: Microservices Approach (Modular)
docs.text: Separate services (sensing, ML, control) communicate via API: - Pros: Flexible, scalable, easy to replace/upgrade - Cons: Networking overhead, more complex deployment

docs.title: Hybrid Approach (Recommended)
docs.text:
• Core control loop: ROS (robotics middleware)
  • ML models: TensorFlow/PyTorch (containerized)
  • Simulation: OpenFOAM (separate compute)
  • LLM reasoning: API call to GPT-4 or Claude (cloud)

docs.title: Example: Closed-Loop Powder Dispensing
docs.text:
Step 1: Sense initial state
  └─ Measure: powder properties (size, density, friction)
  └─ Sensor: rheometer, sieve, scales (takes 2–5 min)

Step 2: Predict parameters via ML
  └─ Input: [size, density, friction]
  └─ Model: trained neural network
  └─ Output: suggested auger speed = 35 rpm ✓

Step 3: Execute with feedback control
  └─ Set auger speed to 35 rpm
  └─ Monitor weight in real time (load cell, 100 Hz)
  └─ PID control: if weight lagging, increase speed; if leading, decrease speed
  └─ Duration: 20 seconds
  └─ Result: 5.0 ± 0.05 g delivered ✓

docs.title: Process Duration: 5–30 seconds
docs.text:
• Sensor latency budget: < 100 ms (feedback must be fast)
  • ML inference time: < 10 ms (quick prediction)
  • Control update rate: 100 Hz = 10 ms per cycle

docs.title: Total system latency
docs.text:
• Sensing: 10 ms
  • ML inference: 5 ms
  • Control computation: 5 ms
  • Actuator response: 50 ms
  • Total: ~70 ms latency (acceptable for most processes)

docs.title: 1. Misalignment Between Sensor & Control
docs.text:
Problem: Sensor accuracy is ±2%, but control target is ±1%

Solution: Ensure sensor is 5× more accurate than control requirement

docs.title: 2. Over-Reliance on ML Without Validation
docs.text:
Problem: Train ML model on simulated data, deploy to real hardware → 20% error

Solution: Always validate ML model on 5–20 real samples before full deployment

docs.title: 3. Control Loop Tuning
docs.text:
Problem: PID gains are "magic numbers"; no one knows how to adjust them

Solution: Use Ziegler-Nichols or model-based tuning method; document gains

docs.title: 4. Sensor Drift
docs.text:
Problem: Load cell calibration drifts over weeks; measurements become unreliable

Solution: Calibrate sensors weekly; implement drift detection (compare to reference)

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Explore each layer in depth:

  • Sensing & Characterization — How to measure material properties
  • Feedback Control — How to implement real-time control loops
  • Machine Learning — How to train models for material handling
  • Digital Twins & LLMs — How to simulate and reason about tasks

docs.title: LLMs & AI Agents
docs.text:
Step 7 · Decide

This page summarizes Section 8.3 and Table 7 of the review. It supersedes the agent discussion on the earlier Digital Twins & LLMs page where the two differ.

docs.title: From models to agents
docs.text:
Large language models (LLMs) extend decision making from numbers to text and code. Through application programming interfaces (APIs), models such as GPT-4 [138] and Claude [139] can:

  • draft hypotheses from the literature and from a laboratory's own results;
  • organize scattered information into structured records;
  • turn a formulation goal into a sequence of operations;
  • support multi-step planning across instruments, databases and calculation tools.

Such agents have planned and run chemical experiments on robots [125], [127], been assessed for chemistry robotics [126] and coordinated multiple robots and instruments [140], [141], [142].

On its own, an LLM produces text. An agentic system wraps the LLM in a loop:

  1. plan;
  2. call tools such as instrument APIs, databases and simulators;
  3. observe the results;
  4. revise the plan.

Coscientist [125] and ChemCrow [127] work this way. For formulation, the most immediate value is in bridging a scientist's intent and an executable protocol, and in explaining what was done and why. Agent outputs still have to be checked before they reach hardware [129], [130], which is the job the digital twin already does.

docs.title: Agents built for SDLs
docs.text: Agent What it does ORGANA Works with chemists to derive experiment goals, resolves ambiguities and keeps experiment logs while planning and running robotic chemistry with visual feedback [172]. ChemAgents Coordinates role-specific agents for literature reading, experiment design, computation and robot operation around a robotic AI chemist [175]. LLM-RDF Assigns specialized agents to literature search, experiment design, hardware execution, spectrum analysis and result interpretation, for end-to-end synthesis development [176]. AILA Automates atomic force microscopy. It comes with a benchmark of the whole workflow, from experimental design to analysis, that shows where current models still fail [177]. CRESt Couples multimodal models and natural-language interaction with robotic synthesis and characterization to discover multi-element electrocatalysts [178]. El Agente Generates and runs quantum-chemistry workflows from natural-language requests (computational) [173]. La Agente Óptima Builds and supervises Bayesian optimization campaigns, keeping LLM reasoning separate from the loop that actually runs. In a closed-loop contact-angle campaign it caught and corrected a mid-run measurement failure. It also concluded that the target could not be reached with the available reagents and recommended a change of formulation [174]. This is the closest example to formulation.

docs.title: Agent roles in a formulation SDL
docs.text:
Inside a formulation SDL, agents are most useful as assistants to the people and deterministic components that already own each decision:

  • Campaign designer. Turns a scientist's goal into a draft campaign (ingredients, bounds, objectives and budget). It runs a dry run of the process plan to check that each seed formulation can be made on the cell before a person approves it.
  • Laboratory copilot. Explains what the cell is doing, why a formulation was rejected or why a motion failed validation.
  • Recovery advisor. After a fault, gathers device states, action logs and events and ranks recovery options for the operator.
  • Results analyst. Explains why the optimizer chose each candidate and drafts reports.
  • Knowledge assistant. Answers questions from standard operating procedures, device manuals and safety data sheets, with citations.

Each agent acts only through tools that the orchestration layer exposes, for example as MCP servers [171], and only with the permissions of the person it serves.

docs.text: Agent Assists Example tasks Autonomy Human checkpoint SDL examples Campaign designer Scientist Goal to draft campaign; dry-run checks of seed formulations Draft; submit only in approved campaigns Scientist approves campaign and runs La Agente Óptima [174]; ChemAgents [175] Laboratory copilot Scientist, operator Explains status, rejections and validation verdicts Inform None (read-only) ORGANA [172]; CRESt [178] Recovery advisor Operator Gathers fault context; ranks recovery options Draft Operator decides the recovery La Agente Óptima [174] Results analyst Scientist, engineer Explains proposals; sandboxed analysis; report drafts Act digitally Author reviews reports LLM-RDF [176]; AILA [177] Knowledge assistant Everyone Cited answers from SOPs, manuals and safety data sheets Inform None (read-only) Coscientist [125]; ChemCrow [127]

docs.title: Levels of autonomy and safeguards
docs.text:
Autonomy is best granted in levels:

  1. Informing: read and explain.
  2. Drafting: make proposals that a person must accept.
  3. Acting digitally: dry runs, simulation and sandboxed analysis.
  4. Submitting experiments, at most, and only inside a campaign a scientist has approved.

Even at the top level, submissions remain subject to the twin's rehearsal and the execution checks of the orchestration software.

Safety by construction, not by instruction

If no tool exists for device commands, arming the cell, editing safety configuration or approving runs, then a prompt injection or a model error can at worst produce a draft, which a person and the deterministic checks will reject.

Two further safeguards matter for formulation data:

  • Route model calls by data class. Confidential formulations and results should only reach self-hosted or institutionally approved models.
  • Evaluate every change. Any change to a prompt, tool or model should pass fixed evaluation suites before deployment: campaign design, tool use, grounded answers, fault recovery and red-team tests. Each agent run should be recorded alongside the experiments it touched.

See also Safety in Autonomous Material Handling.

docs.title: Data & Decision Models
docs.text:
Step 7 · Decide: What to make next?

This page summarizes Sections 8.1–8.2 of the review. Language models and agents are covered on LLMs & AI Agents. The earlier wiki page Machine Learning has practical model-training guidance.

A formulation SDL that can dose, move, mix, rehearse and orchestrate still needs something to decide what to make next. Every such decision depends on the data, models and strategies behind it.

Figure 9. The decision ladder: data (bottom), models that choose the next experiment (middle) and AI agents (top), connected to the robots by software and data pipelines (right).

docs.title: What a formulation experiment records
docs.text:
One experiment produces several kinds of data:

Kind Examples Scalars and labels The recipe and its outcome Time series Balance readings, extrusion pressure, mixing torque, temperature, or the signal of a self-powered sensor [131] Spectra and curves Rheological flow curves, UV-vis or infrared spectra, the acoustic-to-electrical response of an energy-harvesting composite [132] Images and video Foam, phase separation, droplets or powder, as in the vision-guided scenarios [12], [28], [33] Metadata Ingredient lots, instrument settings, trajectories and provenance

The data can also be split by how quickly it is used:

  • Process data has to be acted on by the controller within seconds (see Feedback Control).
  • Property data is what the planner learns from between experiments.

When experiments are stored as FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable) records [133], every experiment can be reused, not just its headline result.

docs.title: Surrogate models and acquisition strategies
docs.text:
The simplest use of these data is a surrogate model. It maps composition and process parameters to measured properties, replacing the lookup table with a prediction.

The decisive step is choosing the next experiment. An acquisition function ranks candidate experiments using the surrogate's predictions and their uncertainty:

  • Active learning samples where the model is least certain [134].
  • Bayesian optimization balances that uncertainty against predicted performance to reach good formulations in few experiments [135]. Libraries such as BoTorch make both routine [136].
  • For small, low-dimensional problems, simpler sequential methods such as simplex optimization still work well [151].

These methods matter most when time, material or instrument hours are scarce, which they always are in a formulation SDL. The handling studies already use them:

  • viscous pipetting [11];
  • powdered-beverage reconstitution [42];
  • Cao et al. combined a classifier with multi-objective Bayesian optimization on robotic platforms and found nine suitable commercial liquid formulations in 15 working days [137].

Handling data belongs in the objective

Engineering measurements such as a dispensing error, a torque trace or a rheology curve can go directly into the objective or the constraints. The planner then learns which recipes the hardware can make reliably, not only which ones perform well.

docs.title: The decision ladder
docs.text:
Data, models and agents form a ladder of decision making (Fig. 9):

  1. structured data;
  2. models that choose the next experiment;
  3. agents that plan whole workflows.

Each rung needs more from the data beneath it, and that is where handling comes back in: a planner can only learn from a dose that was actually delivered and a premix that was actually mixed. Continue to LLMs & AI Agents.

docs.title: Digital Twins & LLMs for Material Handling
docs.text:
Updated to manuscript V3

This page is the earlier wiki's hands-on view. The review's account is on Simulation & Digital Twins (four-level fidelity hierarchy, ROS 2/MoveIt 2, Isaac Sim, Chemistry3D [110], MATTERIX [111], and the twin as a verification gate) and LLMs & AI Agents (agent roles, autonomy levels, MCP tool exposure [171], safety by construction). Where the two differ, the V3 pages take precedence.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Digital twins are high-fidelity simulations of physical systems used for training, validation, and debugging.

Large language models (LLMs) are AI agents that can reason about complex tasks, select strategies, and adapt plans.

Together, they enable autonomous systems to learn and reason in a symbiotic way: simulation provides safe training data; LLM provides high-level reasoning.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A digital twin is a virtual replica of a physical system that responds to inputs in a way that mimics real-world behavior.

In material handling: - Input: equipment parameters (pump speed, pressure, grip force) - Physics: material properties + equipment mechanics - Output: outcome (mass dispensed, force applied, grasp success)

docs.title: Purposes
docs.text:
1. Offline training — Train ML models on 10,000 simulated materials without touching real hardware
  2. Debugging — Reproduce failures in a controlled, repeatable environment
  3. Design exploration — Test new hardware designs before machining
  4. Risk-free learning — Trial-and-error with virtual materials (no waste)

docs.title: Discrete Element Method (DEM) for Powders
docs.text:
Simulates individual particles, their interactions (friction, collision, cohesion).

Physics:

For each particle:
  F = gravity + friction_with_walls + friction_with_neighbors + van_der_Waals
  x, v = integrate(F) using Euler or Verlet

Tools: - LIGGGHTS (open-source, integrated with ParaView visualization) - EDEM (commercial, Altair) - Bullet Physics (robotics-friendly)

Effort to build: 2–4 weeks (if you know DEM); integrating with your control software adds another 2–4 weeks

Validation: Compare simulated vs. real powder flow rate; accuracy ±5–10% with good tuning

Example:

# Pseudocode: simulate auger feeder
particles = initialize_particles(N=10000, size_range=[10, 100], density=1.5)

for timestep in range(100_000):  # ~10 seconds of simulation
    for p in particles:
        # Gravity
        f = p.mass * [0, -9.81]

        # Friction with walls
        if p.touching_hopper_wall:
            f += friction_coeff * normal_force

        # Van der Waals (cohesion)
        for neighbor in p.nearby_particles:
            f += adhesion_energy / distance^2

        # Update position
        p.acceleration = f / p.mass
        p.velocity += p.acceleration * dt
        p.position += p.velocity * dt

    # Rotate auger
    auger.rotate(speed_rpm * dt)
    particles_in_auger.set_velocity(auger.velocity)

    # Count particles exiting
    exiting_particles = [p for p in particles if p.z < exit_height]
    mass_flow = len(exiting_particles) * p.mass

docs.title: Finite Element Method (FEM) for Liquids & Semi-Solids
docs.text:
Solves Navier-Stokes equations on a mesh to compute velocity, pressure, stress.

Tools: - COMSOL Multiphysics (commercial, user-friendly) - OpenFOAM (open-source, powerful, steep learning curve) - Ansys Fluent (commercial, industry standard)

Effort: 4–12 weeks (depending on geometry complexity and desired accuracy)

Example setup:

Domain: 3D syringe barrel + nozzle
Boundary conditions:
  - Inlet: plunger moving at velocity V
  - Outlet: free surface (dynamic)
  - Walls: no-slip
Material model: Herschel-Bulkley (yield-stress + shear-thinning)
  η(γ̇) = τ_y / γ̇ + k * γ̇^(n-1)
Solver: Finite Volume Method, transient, 10,000 mesh elements
Output: velocity field, pressure drop, flow rate Q(t)

docs.title: Rigid Body Dynamics for Solid Handling
docs.text:
Simulates motion, contact, and forces for solid objects and grippers.

Tools: - PyBullet (Python-friendly, real-time) - Isaac Sim (NVIDIA, vision-integrated, photorealistic) - Gazebo (ROS ecosystem, open-source) - Mujoco (DeepMind, differentiable physics)

Effort: 1–2 weeks for basic simulation; weeks–months for accurate friction/contact models

Example:

import pybullet as p
import pybullet_data

client = p.connect(p.GUI)
p.setAdditionalSearchPath(pybullet_data.getDataPath())
p.loadURDF("plane.urdf")

# Create tablet and gripper
tablet = p.loadURDF("tablet.urdf", [0, 0, 0.1])
gripper = p.loadRobot("gripper.urdf", [0, 0, 0.2])

# Simulate
for t in range(1000):
    # Close gripper
    p.setJointMotorControl2(gripper, finger_joint, 
                           p.POSITION_CONTROL, 
                           targetPosition=0.02 + 0.03 * (t / 100))

    # Measure contact force
    contacts = p.getContactPoints(gripper, tablet)
    if contacts:
        force = sum([c[9] for c in contacts])
        print(f"Grip force: {force:.2f} N")

    p.stepSimulation()
    time.sleep(0.01)

docs.title: Step 1: Parametrize Material Space
docs.text:
Define input features that vary across the population:

Powder: [particle_size, density, moisture, friction, cohesion]
Liquid: [viscosity, yield_stress, surface_tension, temperature]
Solid: [shape, mass, surface_friction, elasticity]

docs.title: Step 2: Generate Synthetic Data
docs.text:
N_materials = 1000
materials = []
for i in range(N_materials):
    material = {
        'size': np.random.uniform(10, 500),  # µm
        'density': np.random.uniform(0.8, 2.5),  # g/cm³
        'moisture': np.random.normal(0.03, 0.01),  # %
        'friction': np.random.uniform(0.2, 0.8),
        'cohesion': np.random.exponential(50)  # Pa
    }

    # Run simulator
    result = simulate_auger(material, speed=30_rpm)
    optimal_speed = find_optimal_speed(material, target_mass=5.0)

    materials.append({
        'features': [size, density, moisture, friction, cohesion],
        'target': optimal_speed
    })

# Train ML model on these 1000 examples
X = [m['features'] for m in materials]
y = [m['target'] for m in materials]

model = RandomForestRegressor()
model.fit(X, y)

docs.title: Step 3: Validation on Real Materials
docs.text:
# Test on 5–10 real powders
real_powders = [real_api_1, real_api_2, ..., real_api_5]

for powder in real_powders:
    # Measure properties
    props = measure_properties(powder)

    # Predict
    pred_speed = model.predict([props])

    # Execute
    actual_result = dispense_on_hardware(speed=pred_speed)

    # Compare
    error = abs(actual_result - 5.0)
    print(f"Powder: {error:.2f}g error")

If errors are consistently < 2%, simulator is validated ✓

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Large language models (GPT-4, Claude) can reason about high-level tasks, select strategies, and adapt plans.

Use cases: 1. Task decomposition: "Dispense 10 different APIs" → break into sub-tasks 2. Strategy selection: Given material properties, suggest appropriate control strategy 3. Adaptation: "Powder is cohesive; Strategy 2 (iterate) is failing → switch to Strategy 3 (real-time correction)" 4. Explanation: Justify why a particular dispense failed

docs.title: Agent Architecture
docs.text:
User Goal
  ↓
LLM Agent (GPT-4 / Claude)
  ├─ Task decomposition
  ├─ Consult knowledge base (strategies, hardware specs)
  ├─ Reason about material properties
  ├─ Select best strategy
  ├─ Plan execution steps
  └─ Output: [step 1, step 2, step 3, ...]
    ↓
Execution Layer (ROS, robots, pumps)
  ├─ Execute each step
  ├─ Measure outcomes
  └─ Report back to agent
    ↓
LLM (continued)
  ├─ Assess results
  ├─ If success: done
  ├─ If failure: reason about why, adapt plan
  ├─ Switch strategies if needed
  └─ Retry or escalate

docs.title: Example 1: Dispensing a Novel Powder
docs.text:
User: "I have a new pharmaceutical powder. Dispense 1.0 g accurately."

LLM Agent reasoning:
  1. Task: dispense novel powder
  2. Unknown properties → need characterization first
  3. Available strategies:
     - Strategy 1 (Characterize): measure powder, predict speed
     - Strategy 2 (Iterate): dispense, measure, adjust
     - Strategy 5 (Simulate): use ML model trained on 100 powders
  4. Recommend: 
     - Try Strategy 1 first (fast, if model is available)
     - Fall back to Strategy 2 if accuracy insufficient
     - Use Strategy 3 (real-time correction) if powder is cohesive

Agent output plan:
  Step 1: Measure powder properties (PSD, Hausner ratio, moisture)
  Step 2: Apply trained ML model → predict speed = 35 rpm
  Step 3: Set auger to 35 rpm, dispense, measure
  Step 4: If ±1%, done. Else, switch to iterative feedback control
  Step 5: Log results for model retraining

docs.title: Example 2: Handling Unexpected Failure
docs.text:
LLM observes:
  - Material: API powder
  - Strategy 2 (Iterate) was used
  - After 5 optimization cycles, still ±3% (target ±1%)
  - Pattern: each cycle, mass overshoots then undershoots → system oscillating

LLM reasoning:
  - Iterative optimization hit its limit → material is too cohesive
  - Real-time correction (Strategy 3) may help (faster loop, detect mid-process)
  - Or: Physical reinvention (Strategy 6) needed (switch to vacuum feeder)

LLM decision:
  - Try real-time correction first (10 min, low cost)
  - If still fails: escalate to human (recommend vacuum feeder)

Plan:
  Step 1: Switch control strategy to real-time correction
  Step 2: Set PID gains conservatively
  Step 3: Dispense with live weight feedback
  Step 4: If success, done. Else: inform user, recommend new hardware.

docs.title: Implementing LLM Agents
docs.text:
from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(api_key="sk-...")

def dispense_with_llm_guidance(powder_properties, target_mass=1.0):
    # Step 1: Ask LLM to recommend strategy
    prompt = f"""
    I need to dispense pharmaceutical powder.

    Properties measured:
    - Particle size: {powder_properties['size']} µm
    - Density: {powder_properties['density']} g/cm³
    - Moisture: {powder_properties['moisture']}%
    - Hausner ratio: {powder_properties['hausner']}

    Available strategies:
    1. Characterize: measure then act (5 min, ±5% accuracy)
    2. Iterative: dispense-measure-adjust (15 min, ±1% accuracy)
    3. Real-time: live feedback control (5 min, ±2% accuracy)
    4. Simulation: ML model (1 min, ±3% accuracy)

    Recommend the best strategy and explain why.
    """

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        temperature=0.5
    )

    recommendation = response.choices[0].message.content
    print(f"LLM recommends:\n{recommendation}")

    # Step 2: Execute recommended strategy
    if "Characterize" in recommendation:
        strategy = "characterize"
    elif "Iterative" in recommendation:
        strategy = "iterate"
    elif "Real-time" in recommendation:
        strategy = "real-time"
    else:
        strategy = "simulate"

    result = execute_strategy(strategy, target_mass)

    # Step 3: Report result back to LLM
    if result['accuracy'] > 0.05:  # > ±5% error
        followup = f"""
        Dispensing with strategy '{strategy}' achieved {result['accuracy']:.2%} error.
        This is insufficient. What should I do next?
        - Retry with same strategy?
        - Switch to a different strategy?
        - Modify hardware?
        - Consult human expert?
        """

        followup_response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": followup}],
            temperature=0.5
        )

        next_action = followup_response.choices[0].message.content
        print(f"LLM suggests:\n{next_action}")
    else:
        print(f"Success! Accuracy {result['accuracy']:.2%}")

    return result

docs.title: Digital Twin + LLM Synergy
docs.text:
Scenario: New formulation, no historical data, high accuracy required

Step 1: LLM decides to use simulation-based generalization
         ├─ Train ML model on 500 simulated materials
         ├─ No real-world waste
         └─ Generate training data overnight

Step 2: Validate on real materials
         ├─ LLM selects 3 representative real materials
         ├─ Dispense with predicted parameters
         └─ Compare simulation vs. reality

Step 3: Adapt model
         ├─ LLM detects systematic bias (simulator predicts high)
         ├─ Requests recalibration of simulator's friction model
         ├─ Retrain on new simulated data
         └─ Validate again

Step 4: Deploy
         ├─ LLM confident in model ✓
         ├─ Dispense 1000 batches with ML model
         └─ Monitor accuracy over time

Benefits: - No human guesswork; reasoning is explicit - Leverages simulation for safe training - Adapts when real world differs from simulation - Can explain its decisions

docs.title: Minimal Viable Setup
docs.text:
# 1. ROS-based control system (existing)
# 2. LLM API access (OpenAI, Anthropic)
# 3. Simple strategy dispatcher

strategies = {
    'characterize': CharacterizeStrategy(),
    'iterate': IterativeStrategy(),
    'real-time': RealTimeStrategy(),
    'simulate': SimulationStrategy()
}

def autonomous_dispense(material_properties, target):
    # Consult LLM
    recommended_strategy = query_llm(material_properties)

    # Execute
    strategy_obj = strategies[recommended_strategy]
    result = strategy_obj.execute(material_properties, target)

    # Feedback to LLM
    if result.error > tolerance:
        new_strategy = query_llm(result, material_properties)
        result = strategies[new_strategy].execute(material_properties, target)

    return result

docs.title: Feedback Control
docs.text:
Updated to manuscript V3

In the review, closed-loop correction appears in gravimetric Bayesian-optimized pipetting [11], vision-corrected extrusion bioprinting (~10 s response) [33] and vision-guided powder scooping [12]. The review distinguishes process data, which control must act on within seconds, from property data learned by the planner between experiments (Data & Decision Models).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Feedback control uses sensor measurements to adjust equipment parameters in real-time, keeping the process on target despite disturbances and uncertainties.

docs.title: The Control Loop
docs.text:
Desired Target
       ↓
   [Compare Error]
       ↓ error = target - measured
  [Control Algorithm]  ← compute control action
       ↓
  [Actuate Equipment]  ← adjust pump speed, force, etc.
       ↓
  [Measure State]  ← load cell, F/T sensor, camera
       ↓
   [Feedback] ──→ back to Compare Error

Loop rate: Typically 100 Hz – 1 kHz (update every 10 ms – 1 ms)

docs.title: PID Control (Most Common)
docs.text: Proportional-Integral-Derivative control is the industry standard.

docs.title: Mathematical Form
docs.text:
\[ u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau) d\tau + K_d \frac{de}{dt} \]

Where: - \(u(t)\) = control signal (pump speed, force, pressure) - \(e(t)\) = error = target − measured - \(K_p\) = proportional gain - \(K_i\) = integral gain - \(K_d\) = derivative gain

docs.title: Proportional (P)
docs.text:
\(u = K_p \cdot e\)

  • Responds immediately to error
  • If error is 10% too high, increase speed by \(K_p \times 10\%\)
  • Fast, but can overshoot
  • Too high → oscillation; too low → slow response

docs.title: Integral (I)
docs.text:
\(u_i = K_i \int e \, dt\)

  • Accumulates error over time
  • Corrects steady-state bias
  • Example: If you're consistently 5% short, I term learns this and adds constant offset
  • Too high → slow, oscillatory; too low → residual error

docs.title: Derivative (D)
docs.text:
\(u_d = K_d \frac{de}{dt}\)

  • Responds to rate of change
  • Dampens overshoot
  • Reduces oscillation when P term is aggressive
  • Sensitive to sensor noise; usually needs low-pass filter

docs.title: Method 1: Ziegler-Nichols (Classic)
docs.text:
1. Set \(K_i = K_d = 0\) (P-only mode)
  2. Increase \(K_p\) slowly until system oscillates steadily
  3. Note the critical gain \(K_p^c\) and oscillation period \(T_u\)
  4. Set final gains:
\[ K_p = 0.6 \, K_p^c \] \[ K_i = 1.2 \, K_p^c / T_u \] \[ K_d = 0.075 \, K_p^c \, T_u \]

docs.title: Method 2: Empirical (Trial & Error)
docs.text:
1. Start with conservative \(K_p = 1\)
  2. Run a test, observe response (slow? oscillating?)
  3. Adjust:
  4. If slow: increase \(K_p\) (try 2, 5, 10)
  5. If oscillating: decrease \(K_p\) or increase \(K_d\)
  6. Once P is tuned, add small \(K_i\) (start at \(K_p / 10\))
  7. Refine \(K_d\) to reduce overshoot

docs.title: Method 3: Pole Placement (Advanced)
docs.text:
If you have a model of your system (e.g., transfer function), compute gains to place closed-loop poles at desired locations.

Tools: MATLAB Control System Toolbox, Python control library

docs.title: Example: Auger Feeder with Weight Feedback
docs.text:
# Pseudo-code for PID loop
Kp = 5   # rpm per gram error
Ki = 1   # integral term
Kd = 0.5 # derivative dampening

target_mass = 5.0  # grams
error_integral = 0
error_prev = 0

for t in range(0, 30_seconds, dt=10ms):
    measured_mass = load_cell.read()
    error = target_mass - measured_mass

    # Compute PID
    P = Kp * error
    I = Ki * error_integral
    D = Kd * (error - error_prev) / dt

    speed = 30 + P + I + D  # 30 rpm is nominal
    speed = max(10, min(50, speed))  # Constrain to [10, 50] rpm

    auger.set_speed(speed)

    # Update state
    error_integral += error * dt
    error_prev = error

    if abs(error) < 0.05:  # Within 0.05 g tolerance
        break  # Dosing complete

docs.title: Typical Response
docs.text:
Time  Target  Measured  Error  Speed(rpm)  Action
---   ---     ---       ---    ---         ---
0 s   5.0g    0.0g      5.0g   40          Start, increase
2 s   5.0g    1.5g      3.5g   40          Continuing
4 s   5.0g    3.2g      1.8g   35          Slow down (error decreasing)
6 s   5.0g    4.5g      0.5g   30          Almost there
7 s   5.0g    4.95g     0.05g  28          ✓ Within tolerance
7.1 s 5.0g    5.02g    -0.02g  27          ✓ Still good, stop

docs.title: Force Control (Gripping)
docs.text: For robots holding fragile objects, maintain constant grip force (not position).

docs.title: Example: Holding a Tissue Sample
docs.text:
Kp_force = 2  # Increase opening by 0.1 mm per 0.5 N excess force
target_force = 2.0  # Newtons (gentle grip)

for t in range(0, hold_duration, dt=50ms):
    measured_force = wrist_sensor.force_z()
    error_force = target_force - measured_force

    finger_position += Kp_force * error_force

    gripper.set_position(finger_position)

    if measured_force > 5.0:  # Overload!
        print("WARNING: Force exceeds 5 N, object may be damaged")
        gripper.open()  # Emergency release

Outcome: Tissue is gripped at constant 2 N, preventing bruise damage from excessive pressure.

docs.title: Adaptive Control
docs.text: Parameters change as the system/material changes.

docs.title: Example: High-Viscosity Liquid Extrusion
docs.text:
# Model: Extrusion rate depends on applied pressure and material viscosity
# Q = (P - τ_y) / (η × L)  [Hagen-Poiseuille + yield stress]

def adaptive_pressure_control(target_flow_rate):
    # Measure viscosity every 10 seconds (rheometer on sample)
    if t % 10 == 0:
        eta = rheometer.measure_viscosity()

    # Adaptive model: compute pressure needed for target flow
    required_pressure = target_flow_rate * (eta + yield_stress / flow_constant)

    # Apply with feedback correction
    measured_flow = flowmeter.read()
    error = target_flow_rate - measured_flow

    pressure = required_pressure + Kp * error
    pump.set_pressure(pressure)

Benefit: As viscosity changes (temperature drift, solvent evaporation), control automatically adjusts pressure.

docs.title: Problem 1: Sensor Noise → Noisy Control Signal
docs.text:
Symptom: Load cell reads 4.98, 5.02, 4.99, 5.01 g; control signal oscillates wildly

Solution: Add low-pass filter before PID:

filtered_error = 0.8 * filtered_error + 0.2 * raw_error  # Exponential moving average

docs.title: Problem 2: Saturation (Actuator Limits)
docs.text:
Symptom: PID computes speed = 200 rpm, but pump max is 100 rpm; system clips and behaves weirdly

Solution: Anti-windup (constrain integrator when saturated):

if speed > MAX_SPEED:
    speed = MAX_SPEED
    error_integral = error_integral - Ki * error  # Unwind integrator

docs.title: Problem 3: Time Delay / Lag
docs.text:
Symptom: 500 ms delay between setting pump speed and seeing mass change; control oscillates

Solution: Predict future state (model-based control):

# Predict state 500 ms into future
predicted_mass = current_mass + flowrate * 0.5
error = target - predicted_mass
control = Kp * error + Ki * integral

docs.title: Cascade Control (Nested Loops)
docs.text:
When you have two control objectives (e.g., dispense amount AND dispense speed):

Outer loop: maintains total dispensed mass
  ↓
Inner loop: maintains instantaneous flow rate

Example:
  Target: dispense 10 g total at 0.5 g/s

  Outer: If we've dispensed 8 g and need 2 more, maintain speed = 0.5 g/s
  Inner: If current speed is 0.4 g/s, increase pump pressure to reach 0.5 g/s

docs.title: State Machine Control (Discrete Logic)
docs.text:
For processes with distinct phases, use state machines rather than continuous PID:

State 0: Startup
  └─ Set pump to nominal speed
  └─ Wait for flow to stabilize (2 seconds)
  └─ Transition to State 1

State 1: Controlled Dosing
  └─ PID loop maintains weight
  └─ If error < 0.1%, go to State 2

State 2: Stopping
  └─ Ramp down speed to zero (no jerk)
  └─ Wait 1 second for settling
  └─ Done

docs.title: Simulation & Validation
docs.text:
Before deploying control on real hardware:

  1. Simulate your system's response (use model, or just guess)
  2. Tune gains in simulation
  3. Test on real hardware with conservative gains
  4. Observe real response, compare to simulation
  5. Refine gains if needed
# Simulation
class PowderFeeder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.mass = 0

    def step(self, speed_rpm, dt):
        flow_rate = 0.1 * speed_rpm  # Simplified: 0.1 g/sec per rpm
        self.mass += flow_rate * dt

# Test control tuning offline
feeder = PowderFeeder()
for t in range(100):
    error = 5.0 - feeder.mass
    speed = 30 + 5 * error  # Kp = 5
    feeder.step(speed, dt=0.1)
    print(f"t={t} mass={feeder.mass:.2f} speed={speed:.0f}")

docs.title: Implementation Checklist
docs.text:
• Define control objective (what are you controlling? weight? force? position?)
  • Select sensor(s) with appropriate bandwidth and accuracy
  • Choose control algorithm (PID? State machine? Adaptive?)
  • Simulate control loop offline
  • Tune gains (Ziegler-Nichols or empirically)
  • Implement in software (ROS, LabVIEW, Python)
  • Test on real hardware at low intensity (conservative gains)
  • Observe response, refine gains
  • Validate on 5–10 representative materials
  • Document gains and assumptions for future reference

docs.title: Machine Learning for Material Handling
docs.text:
Updated to manuscript V3

The review frames ML for formulation SDLs around surrogate models plus acquisition functions: active learning [134], Bayesian optimization [135] (e.g. BoTorch [136]) and, for small problems, simplex methods [151]. Examples: viscous pipetting [11], powdered-beverage reconstitution [42], and nine commercial liquid formulations found in 15 working days with a classifier plus multi-objective BO [137]. See Data & Decision Models.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Machine learning enables systems to learn from past experience and generalize to new, unseen materials. Key applications: predicting optimal parameters, classifying materials, adapting control strategies.

docs.title: Supervised Learning (Most Common)
docs.text:
Train a model with labeled examples: (input, target_output) pairs.

Application: Predict pump speed from measured viscosity

Input: viscosity (cP)  →  Output: optimal pump speed (rpm)

Training data:
  1 cP    → 80 rpm
  2 cP    → 78 rpm
  5 cP    → 70 rpm
  10 cP   → 60 rpm
  50 cP   → 40 rpm
  100 cP  → 30 rpm

Model: learns a function f(viscosity) → speed
Test: on new material with 8 cP, predict speed ≈ 65 rpm ✓

docs.title: Unsupervised Learning
docs.text:
Find patterns in unlabeled data.

Application: Cluster powder types by flowability

Input: [particle_size, density, moisture] (no labels)

Clustering result:
  Cluster 1: Large, dense, dry   → free-flowing
  Cluster 2: Fine, light, moist  → cohesive

New powder: measure properties → assign to Cluster 1 → use high-speed auger

docs.title: Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
Learn by trial-and-error; agent takes actions and receives rewards/penalties.

Application: Optimize gripper finger positions to maximize grasp stability

State: object shape, gripper position
Action: adjust finger position by ±1 mm
Reward: grasp stability (1 = success, 0 = slip)

Agent: learns policy π(state) → best_action through 1000s of trials

docs.title: Regression Models (Continuous Output)
docs.text: Predict a continuous value (speed, pressure, position).

docs.title: Linear Regression
docs.text:
Simplest model: output is linear in input.

\[ y = a + b \, x \]

Pros: Fast, interpretable, needs few examples (5–10)

Cons: Fails for nonlinear relationships

Example: Viscosity → pump speed

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
X = [[1], [2], [5], [10], [50], [100]]  # viscosity (cP)
y = [80, 78, 70, 60, 40, 30]  # optimal speed (rpm)

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)
predicted_speed = model.predict([[8]])  # viscosity = 8 cP
# Output: 64.2 rpm (reasonable)

docs.title: Polynomial Regression
docs.text:
Allow curved relationship: \(y = a + bx + cx^2 + \ldots\)

Pros: Fits nonlinear data better

Cons: Overfits if degree too high; less interpretable

Example: Pressure vs. extrusion rate (nonlinear yield stress effect)

from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
X = [[50], [100], [150], [200]]  # pressure (kPa)
y = [0.1, 0.4, 1.0, 1.9]  # flow rate (mL/s) [nonlinear!]

poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=2)
X_poly = poly.fit_transform(X)

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X_poly, y)
predicted_flow = model.predict(poly.transform([[120]]))
# Captures nonlinearity better than linear

docs.title: Neural Networks (Deep Learning)
docs.text:
Black-box nonlinear model; very flexible.

Pros: Learns complex patterns; generalizes well with enough data

Cons: Needs 100–1000 training examples; hard to interpret; prone to overfitting

Example: Powder properties → optimal auger speed

import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers

# Input: [particle_size, density, moisture, friction]
# Output: [auger_speed, confidence]

model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    layers.Dense(64, activation='relu', input_shape=(4,)),
    layers.Dense(32, activation='relu'),
    layers.Dense(1, activation='linear')
])

model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='mse')
model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=50, validation_split=0.2)

predicted_speed = model.predict([[15, 1.5, 0.05, 0.6]])[0]

docs.title: Gaussian Process Regression
docs.text:
Probabilistic model; gives prediction + uncertainty.

Pros: Provides confidence bounds; works with small datasets (20–100)

Cons: Slow for large datasets; harder to integrate into real-time control

Example: Identify if new powder is "well-understood" or "novel"

from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessRegressor
from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import RBF, ConstantKernel as C

kernel = C(1.0, (1e-3, 1e3)) * RBF(1.0, (1e-2, 1e2))
gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel=kernel, n_restarts_optimizer=10)

gp.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred, sigma = gp.predict(X_test, return_std=True)

# If sigma > 0.5 rpm, prediction is uncertain; use feedback control instead

docs.title: Classification Models (Categorical Output)
docs.text: Predict a class (powder type, defect present/absent, strategy to use).

docs.title: Decision Trees & Random Forests
docs.text:
Simple rule-based model.

Pros: Interpretable, fast training and inference, handles nonlinearity

Cons: Prone to overfitting (shallow) or slow (deep)

Example: Classify powder flowability

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

# Input features
X = [
    [10, 1.2, 0.02],  # particle size (µm), density (g/cm³), moisture (%)
    [100, 1.5, 0.05],
    # ... 20 more examples ...
]

# Target classes
y = ['free-flowing', 'cohesive', 'free-flowing', 'cohesive', ...]

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, max_depth=5)
rf.fit(X, y)

new_powder = [15, 1.3, 0.03]
predicted_class = rf.predict([new_powder])  # 'free-flowing'

docs.title: Support Vector Machines (SVM)
docs.text:
Linear or kernel-based classifier.

Pros: Works well in high dimensions; robust to outliers

Cons: Slow for large datasets; sensitive to scaling

Example: Defect detection (crack vs. intact tablet)

from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Input: tactile signature [contact_force, curvature, stiffness]
X = [[2.5, 0.8, 150], [2.6, 0.75, 145], [1.2, 2.0, 50], ...]
y = ['intact', 'intact', 'cracked', ...]

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)

svm = SVC(kernel='rbf', C=1.0)
svm.fit(X_scaled, y)

new_tablet = scaler.transform([[2.4, 0.82, 148]])
prediction = svm.predict(new_tablet)  # 'intact'

docs.title: 1. Collect Data
docs.text:
Gather (input, target) pairs from real experiments or simulation.

Minimum examples: 10–20 (linear regression), 50–100 (tree-based), 500+ (neural networks)

Material Type | Viscosity (cP) | Optimal Speed (rpm) | Result (g)
-------------|----------------|-------------------|----------
Liquid A     | 1.2            | 80                | 5.00 ± 0.05
Liquid B     | 3.5            | 75                | 4.98 ± 0.03
Liquid C     | 50             | 40                | 5.02 ± 0.08
...

docs.title: 2. Split into Train/Validation/Test
docs.text:
• Training set (70%): Use to fit model parameters
  • Validation set (15%): Use to tune hyperparameters (learning rate, tree depth, etc.)
  • Test set (15%): Use to estimate generalization performance

docs.title: 3. Preprocess Data
docs.text:
Normalize or scale inputs if they have different units/ranges:

# Example: features are [viscosity (1–1000 cP), temp (20–40°C)]
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)  # Mean 0, std 1

# Train model on scaled data
model.fit(X_scaled, y)

# When predicting new data, scale it too
new_data_scaled = scaler.transform(new_data)
prediction = model.predict(new_data_scaled)

docs.title: 4. Train Model
docs.text:
Fit parameters to minimize loss (mean squared error, cross-entropy, etc.).

model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

docs.title: 5. Evaluate
docs.text:
Measure generalization error on validation and test sets:

\[ \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2} \] \[ \text{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2} \] 
y_pred_val = model.predict(X_val)
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((y_val - y_pred_val)**2))
print(f"RMSE on validation set: {rmse:.3f} rpm")

docs.title: 6. Hyperparameter Tuning
docs.text:
Adjust model hyperparameters (tree depth, learning rate, etc.) to minimize validation error.

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

param_grid = {
    'n_estimators': [50, 100, 200],
    'max_depth': [3, 5, 10],
    'min_samples_split': [2, 5]
}

grid = GridSearchCV(RandomForestRegressor(), param_grid, cv=5)
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)

best_model = grid.best_estimator_
print(f"Best params: {grid.best_params_}")

docs.title: 7. Final Validation on Test Set
docs.text:
Evaluate on held-out test data to estimate real-world performance.

y_test_pred = model.predict(X_test)
test_rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((y_test - y_test_pred)**2))
print(f"Test RMSE: {test_rmse:.3f} rpm")
print(f"Test R²: {model.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}")

docs.title: Integration into Control System
docs.text:
# Load trained model
import joblib
model = joblib.load('speed_predictor_model.pkl')

# In real-time control loop
for material in incoming_materials:
    viscosity = measure_viscosity(material)
    predicted_speed = model.predict([[viscosity]])[0]

    feeder.set_speed(predicted_speed)
    actual_result = run_dispensing()

    # Log for future retraining
    log_data(viscosity, predicted_speed, actual_result)

docs.title: Monitoring Model Performance
docs.text:
Track prediction error over time:

Week 1: avg error = 1.2 rpm (good)
Week 2: avg error = 1.5 rpm (acceptable)
Week 3: avg error = 2.8 rpm (degradation!)
  → Investigate: viscosity sensor drifted? Material changed?
  → Retrain model or recalibrate sensor

docs.title: Retraining Schedule
docs.text:
• Weekly: Check prediction errors; flag if drift detected
  • Monthly: Retrain on accumulated data if error > threshold
  • Quarterly: Full pipeline review; check for domain shift

docs.title: 1. Overfitting
docs.text:
Problem: Model fits training data perfectly, but fails on new data

Symptom: Training RMSE = 0.1 rpm, test RMSE = 5 rpm

Solution: - Use regularization (penalize complexity) - Increase training data - Reduce model complexity (shallower tree, smaller network)

docs.title: 2. Domain Shift
docs.text:
Problem: Model trained on water; deployed on organic solvents; accuracy drops

Solution: - Train on diverse materials (not just one family) - Monitor prediction confidence; use fallback strategy if uncertain

docs.title: 3. Insufficient Training Data
docs.text:
Problem: Trained on 5 examples; model is random noise

Solution: - Collect 50+ examples for tree-based models - Use simulation data if real data is scarce - Use transfer learning (pre-train on related task)

docs.title: 4. Ignoring Sensor Noise
docs.text:
Problem: Model trained on "perfect" simulated data; real sensors are noisy; model's performance degrades

Solution: - Train on noisy data (add Gaussian noise to simulation) - Use robust loss functions (e.g., Huber loss instead of MSE)

docs.title: Implementation Checklist
docs.text:
• Define prediction task (input features, output target)
  • Collect training data (50–500 examples, depending on method)
  • Exploratory data analysis (plot features vs. output, look for patterns)
  • Preprocess: normalize, handle missing values, outliers
  • Split: 70% train, 15% val, 15% test
  • Select model (linear? tree? neural net?)
  • Train on training set
  • Tune hyperparameters using validation set
  • Evaluate on test set
  • Check for overfitting; regularize if needed
  • Integrate into control software
  • Monitor performance in production
  • Retrain quarterly or if error drifts
