docs.title: Sensing & Characterization
docs.text:
Updated to manuscript V3

The review emphasizes in-situ sensing that replaces separate characterization: viscosity from pipetting mass flow [22] or dispense time [23], from stirring forces [31] or filmed flow [28]; extrusion monitored by computer vision [33]; powder volume verified by vision during scooping [12]. A formulation experiment also records time series (balance, pressure, torque, self-powered sensor signals [131]) and spectra such as the acoustic-to-electrical response of energy-harvesting composites [132]; see Data & Decision Models.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Before any control strategy can work, you must measure what you're trying to control. This page covers sensors and characterization techniques for material properties and process state.

docs.title: 1. Material Property Sensors (Offline)
docs.text: Used to characterize materials before the main task. Typically take 30 seconds to 5 minutes per measurement.

docs.title: Viscosity/Rheology
docs.text:
• Rotational rheometer (Anton Paar, TA Instruments, Brookfield)
  • Cost: $50k–$150k
  • Measurement time: 2–10 minutes
  • Accuracy: ±1–2%
  • Output: viscosity vs. shear rate curve (full flow behavior)
  • Vibrational viscometer (falling ball, tuning fork)
  • Cost: $5k–$20k
  • Measurement time: 30 seconds
  • Accuracy: ±2–5%
  • Output: single viscosity value at defined shear rate

docs.title: Particle Size & Flowability
docs.text:
• Laser diffraction (Malvern Mastersizer)
  • Cost: $30k–$80k
  • Measurement time: 2 minutes
  • Accuracy: ±2–5%
  • Output: particle size distribution (PSD)
  • Powder rheometer (FT4 Freeman Technology)
  • Cost: $60k–$100k
  • Measurement time: 5 minutes
  • Accuracy: Empirical (not absolute)
  • Output: flowability indices (BFE, SI, HR)
  • Sieve analysis (manual)
  • Cost: $500
  • Measurement time: 30 minutes
  • Accuracy: ±5%
  • Output: cumulative PSD at discrete size bins

docs.title: Moisture Content
docs.text:
• Moisture analyzer (Karl Fischer, loss-on-drying)
  • Cost: $5k–$20k
  • Measurement time: 5 minutes
  • Accuracy: ±0.01%
  • Output: water content (%w/w)

docs.title: Spectroscopy
docs.text:
• UV-Vis spectrometer (PerkinElmer, Shimadzu)
  • Cost: $10k–$50k
  • Measurement time: 1 minute
  • Accuracy: ±1%
  • Output: absorbance at wavelengths (→ concentration via Beer-Lambert)
  • FTIR (Fourier Transform Infrared)
  • Cost: $20k–$80k
  • Measurement time: 2 minutes
  • Accuracy: Qualitative or semi-quantitative
  • Output: chemical composition fingerprint

docs.title: 2. Process State Sensors (Online)
docs.text: Used during the main task to monitor progress and enable feedback control. Typical sampling rates 100 Hz – 1 kHz.

docs.title: Gravimetric (Weight)
docs.text:
• Precision balance (Mettler-Toledo XPE)
  • Cost: $3k–$10k
  • Range: 0–610 g
  • Accuracy: ±0.001 g (1 mg)
  • Bandwidth: 10 Hz (slow for real-time, but typical)
  • Use: Powder dosing feedback
  • Load cell (compression or tension)
  • Cost: $100–$1k
  • Range: 1 kg – 500 kg
  • Accuracy: ±0.1% of range
  • Bandwidth: 100–500 Hz (fast)
  • Use: Real-time weight measurement, gripper force detection

docs.title: Force & Torque
docs.text:
• 6-axis F/T sensor (ATI, Schunk, JR3)
  • Cost: $2k–$10k
  • Range: ±500 N, ±50 N·m (various models)
  • Accuracy: ±1% of full scale
  • Bandwidth: 500 Hz – 2 kHz
  • Use: Extrusion pressure feedback, gripper force control, contact detection

docs.title: Pressure
docs.text:
• Pressure transducer (Honeywell, Hydac)
  • Cost: $200–$500
  • Range: 0–10 bar (typical)
  • Accuracy: ±0.5% FS
  • Bandwidth: 100–500 Hz
  • Use: Syringe pressure, pump outlet pressure, pneumatic feedback

docs.title: Flow Rate
docs.text:
• Coriolis flowmeter (Micro Motion)
  • Cost: $5k–$15k
  • Range: 0.001–50 kg/min
  • Accuracy: ±0.5%
  • Bandwidth: 50 Hz
  • Use: Extrusion rate monitoring
  • Turbine flowmeter
  • Cost: $500–$2k
  • Range: Tunable per design
  • Accuracy: ±1–2%
  • Bandwidth: 100–500 Hz
  • Use: Liquid pumping feedback

docs.title: Displacement & Position
docs.text:
• Linear encoder / LVDT (Linear Variable Differential Transformer)
  • Cost: $300–$1k
  • Range: Typically 0–100 mm
  • Accuracy: ±0.1 mm
  • Bandwidth: 100 Hz – 10 kHz
  • Use: Syringe plunger position, gripper finger displacement
  • Potentiometer (rotary or linear)
  • Cost: $50–$200
  • Accuracy: ±2–5%
  • Bandwidth: Very high (> 10 kHz)
  • Use: Budget feedback, less critical measurements

docs.title: Standard Camera
docs.text:
• USB camera (generic)
  • Cost: $50–$500
  • Resolution: 640×480 – 4K
  • Frame rate: 30–120 fps
  • Latency: 50–100 ms
  • Use: Object detection, fill level monitoring
  • Industrial camera (Basler, FLIR)
  • Cost: $1k–$5k
  • Resolution: 1K – 4K
  • Frame rate: 60–500 fps (high-speed options)
  • Latency: 10–20 ms
  • Use: High-speed process monitoring, real-time feedback

docs.title: Depth Camera
docs.text:
• RealSense / Kinect (structured light)
  • Cost: $100–$500
  • Depth range: 0.1–10 m
  • Accuracy: ±2–5 mm
  • Frame rate: 30–90 fps
  • Use: 3D object detection, bin picking
  • LiDAR (time-of-flight)
  • Cost: $500–$5k
  • Depth range: 0.1–100 m
  • Accuracy: ±5–50 mm (depends on model)
  • Frame rate: 10–20 Hz
  • Use: 3D scene reconstruction, large-scale mapping

docs.title: Temperature
docs.text:
• Thermistor / RTD (Resistance Temperature Detector)
  • Cost: $10–$100
  • Accuracy: ±0.1–1°C
  • Bandwidth: 10 Hz
  • Use: Viscosity correction (viscosity drops ~2% per °C)

docs.title: Humidity
docs.text:
• Capacitive humidity sensor
  • Cost: $20–$100
  • Accuracy: ±2–5% RH
  • Bandwidth: 10 Hz
  • Use: Moisture-sensitive powder properties

docs.title: Sensor Accuracy Requirements
docs.text:
Key rule: Sensor accuracy should be 5–10× better than your control tolerance.

Example: - Target dosing accuracy: ±1% - Required sensor accuracy: ±0.1–0.2% - Implication: A 5 g target requires ±5–10 mg sensor accuracy - Load cell with ±1% accuracy (typically ±50 mg at 5 kg range) is marginal - Better: Use a precision scale with ±1 mg accuracy

docs.title: Sensor Fusion
docs.text: Combining multiple sensors improves reliability:

docs.title: Example: Powder Dispensing
docs.text:
Approach 1: Weight only - Use load cell - Update frequency: 100 Hz - Latency: 10 ms - Robustness: Fails if scale drifts

Approach 2: Weight + vision (fill level) - Load cell provides primary feedback - Camera measures fill height as secondary check - If weight and fill level don't match, flag error - Robustness: Redundancy catches scale drift

Approach 3: Weight + flow meter - Load cell measures total accumulated mass - Flow meter measures instantaneous flow rate - Fuse both: if flow meter says "too slow" but weight is on target, feeder may be slowing down - Robustness: Predictive error detection

docs.title: Load Cell Calibration
docs.text:
1. Zero calibration: With no load, set reading to 0
  2. Span calibration: With known weight (e.g., 5 kg), set reading to 5 kg
  3. Linearity check: Test at 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of range
  4. Frequency: Weekly for production equipment, monthly for lab

docs.title: Vision System Calibration
docs.text:
1. Camera intrinsics: Focal length, principal point, distortion (one-time, or if lens changes)
  2. Camera extrinsics: Position and orientation relative to robot base (one-time or weekly)
  3. Lighting: Consistent illumination (check if shadows change with time of day)

docs.title: Rheometer Calibration
docs.text:
1. Geometry calibration: Empty spindle, verify torque = 0
  2. Temperature control: Peltier element stabilized to ±0.1°C
  3. Standard material: Test on reference fluid (e.g., silicone oil, known viscosity)

docs.title: Sensor Selection Checklist
docs.text:
For your material handling task, answer:

  • What variable am I trying to control? (weight, force, fill level, etc.)
  • What is my target accuracy? (±0.1%, ±1%, ±5%, etc.)
  • What is my process duration? (seconds vs. minutes)
  • What sensor bandwidth do I need? (10 Hz, 100 Hz, 1 kHz?)
  • What is my budget per sensor? ($100, $1k, $10k?)
  • Do I need multiple sensors (redundancy/fusion)?
  • What is my calibration maintenance plan? (weekly, monthly, quarterly)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Rastegardoost, M. M.; Bao, Z.; Sadr, S.; Abdollahi, N.; Darvish, K.; Clasky, A.; Ohsaka, H.; Le Devedec, F. Self-Driving Laboratories for Formulation: Handling Liquids, Pastes, Powders and Objects, from Robots to Digital Twins and AI Agents. Manuscript in preparation, 2026.
  • Key references from the review: [12], [22], [23], [28], [31], [33], [131], [132]. Full list on the References page.

docs.text:
• ISO 13320: Particle size analysis – Laser diffraction method
  • ISO 6440: Vegetable fats and oils – Determination of viscosity
  • NIST Traceability Certificate (for calibration standards)

docs.title: Commercial Hardware: Technologies and Systems
docs.text:
Updated to manuscript V3

Sourced accuracy and price data from the review now live on three pages: Commercial Dispensers (Table 3), Integrated Platforms (Table 4) and Robot Classes (Table 2); low-cost extensions are on Retrofits. The review's main finding: price tracks mechanism class and ecosystem rather than accuracy, and outside liquid handling it is rarely public. The vendor tables of the earlier wiki have been replaced by the review's sourced product list; component and setup cost estimates further down remain illustrative.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This section surveys commercial material handling equipment available for autonomous formulation. Technologies are organized by yield stress (defining material class) and by strategy employed.

docs.title: Taxonomy by Material Class and Yield Stress
docs.text:
Yield Stress Range: 10⁰ – 10⁹ Pa

LIQUIDS (10⁰–10³ Pa)
  ├─ Pipettes & air-displacement systems
  ├─ Syringes & positive-displacement
  ├─ Peristaltic pumps
  ├─ Acoustic dispensing
  └─ Electrospray systems

SEMI-SOLIDS (10²–10⁵ Pa)
  ├─ Screw extrusion systems
  ├─ Air-pressure syringes
  ├─ Progressive cavity pumps
  └─ Piston extruders

POWDERS (10⁴–10⁶ Pa)
  ├─ Auger feeders (volumetric)
  ├─ Vibratory hoppers
  ├─ Vacuum aspiration systems
  ├─ Fluidized-bed dispensers
  └─ Gravimetric feedback systems

SOLIDS (10⁶–10⁹ Pa)

  └─ Vision & force-feedback systems

docs.title: Hardware Organized by Material Type
docs.text:
Updated to manuscript V3

Mechanism descriptions below are from the earlier wiki. Accuracy, cost and vendor lines for which the review gives sourced values have been updated; remaining ranges are illustrative. For named products see Commercial Dispensers and Integrated Platforms; for robots see Robot Classes.

docs.title: Air-Displacement Pipettes
docs.text:
Principle: Movable piston creates air gap above liquid; changes in air volume precisely push/pull liquid.

Accuracy: <1% for water-like liquids on standard robots; Rainin E4 XLS+ ±0.8%, Eppendorf Xplorer ~±0.6% [59], [60] Speed: 30 sec per 10 mL Cost: $191–350 (Rainin E4 XLS+) to ~$1,300 (Eppendorf Xplorer) per pipette [59], [60]

Vendors: Eppendorf, Rainin, Gilson, Hamilton

Suitable materials: Water, solvents, dilute solutions; with slowed aspiration/dispensing and settling delays, up to ~1,000–1,400 cP (99% glycerol) on unmodified Opentrons GEN2 pipettes [21]

Limitations: Viscous liquids need hand-tuned per-liquid settings; volatile solvents evaporate into the air cushion; cannot handle yield-stress materials

docs.title: Syringe Pumps
docs.text:
Principle: Motor drives syringe plunger at controlled speed; linear displacement → precise volume flow.

Accuracy: ±2–5% typical; Hamilton PSD/4 OEM syringe pump ±1% [62] Speed: 5–30 sec per 10 mL (depends on speed setting) Cost: $400–500 (Hamilton PSD/4, OEM) to several $k per benchtop pump [62]

Vendors: Hamilton, New Era

Suitable materials: Low- to medium-viscosity liquids, some semi-solids

Advantages: Versatile, works on bench top, good for research

docs.title: Peristaltic Pumps
docs.text:
Principle: Rotating rollers squeeze flexible tubing; material never touches pump.

Accuracy: ±1% dosing accuracy for precision pumps (Watson-Marlow Qdos 20); generic tubing pumps drift with tubing wear [63] Speed: Tunable, 1–1000 mL/min Cost: $4,248 (Qdos 20) to ~$9,000 (Masterflex L/S Digital) [63], [64]

Vendors: Watson-Marlow, Cole-Parmer / Avantor (Masterflex)

Suitable materials: Any liquid (food-grade, sterile, corrosive); semi-solids at low rates

Advantages: No contact, aseptic, continuous flow

docs.title: Acoustic Droplet Ejection (ADE)
docs.text:
Principle: Focused acoustic transducer creates pressure pulse; ejects nano-droplets from well plate.

Accuracy: <10% transfer accuracy, <8% CV (Echo 525) [80] Speed: Milliseconds per droplet Cost: No public price [80]

Vendors: Beckman Coulter (Labcyte) Echo

Suitable materials: Aqueous solutions, low-viscosity liquids

Advantages: Contactless; useful for fragile reagents (proteins, cells)

Limitations: Expensive; transfer range 25 nL–5 µL (Echo 525) [80]; not for viscous liquids. Research prototypes such as a self-focusing acoustic pipet reach picoliter volumes [24]

docs.title: Screw Extrusion (Stepper Motor)
docs.text:
Principle: Stepper motor drives rotating screw; screw flutes push material out.

Accuracy: ±2–5% (depends on material uniformity) Speed: 10–60 sec per mL Cost: $3k–$15k

Vendors: ViscoTec (preeflow eco-PEN300, ±1%, quote only) [68], Fisnar (PDV-1000) [69]

Suitable materials: Bio-inks, pastes, gels, highly viscous liquids

Advantages: Decouples flow from applied pressure; good control

docs.title: Air-Pressure Syringes
docs.text:
Principle: Compressed air pushes on syringe plunger; material is extruded through nozzle.

Accuracy: ±5–15% (sensitive to pressure fluctuations) Speed: 5–30 sec per mL Cost: $2k–$8k (syringe + regulator)

Vendors: Nordson EFD (Ultimus V, ~$6,750) [17], CELLINK (BIO X pneumatic printhead, $2,500) [67], Allevi (3D Systems) [66]

Suitable materials: Pastes, gels, gentle on cells (low shear)

Advantages: Gentle, no motor vibration; good for bio-inks

Limitations: Pressure fluctuation → volume variation; requires fast feedback for ±1%

docs.title: Progressive Cavity Pumps
docs.text:
Principle: Single rotating screw in elliptical cavity; creates expanding cells that push fluid.

Accuracy: ±1–3% Speed: Tunable, 10–1000 mL/min Cost: $5k–$20k

Vendors: Mono, Netzsch

Suitable materials: High-viscosity, yield-stress, shear-sensitive materials

Advantages: Gentle pumping action; excellent for viscous polymers, cells

docs.title: Auger / Screw Feeders
docs.text:
Principle: Rotating screw conveys powder from hopper to exit; volume per revolution ≈ constant.

Accuracy: ±2–8% (depends on flowability) Speed: 10–30 sec per gram Cost: $2k–$10k

Vendors: Coperion K-Tron (MT12 twin-screw micro-feeder, ~$9,800 secondary market) [70], Chemspeed (SWILE / GDU-P, quote only) [71]

Suitable materials: Free-flowing to moderately cohesive powders

Limitations: Fails with bridging powders; accuracy limited by slip

Improvement: Variable-pitch screws, vacuum assist

docs.title: Vibratory Hoppers
docs.text:
Principle: Vibrating bin loosens powder; gravity feeds through metered orifice.

Accuracy: ±5–15% (poor for cohesive materials) Speed: Fast, 2–10 sec per gram Cost: $1k–$5k

Vendors: 3P Innovation (VF1, ±1 mg dose accuracy) [73], Eriez (Hi-Vi Volumatic) [74]

Suitable materials: Free-flowing powders only

Limitations: Electrostatic buildup; poor accuracy; doesn't work for sticky powders

docs.title: Vacuum-Assisted Dosing
docs.text:
Principle: Suction creates vacuum through metered orifice; powder is pulled out by air flow.

Accuracy: ±1–3% Speed: 10–20 sec per gram Cost: $5k–$15k

Vendors: Research example: tuned vacuum flow and orifice size gave ≤0.1% RSD milligram transfers for one powder [37]

Suitable materials: Cohesive and fine powders; even electrostatic materials

Advantages: Works with difficult powders; good accuracy

docs.title: Fluidized-Bed Dispensers
docs.text:
Principle: Air flows up through porous membrane; powder floats weightless; exit through calibrated nozzle.

Accuracy: ±0.5–2% (excellent) Speed: 10–30 sec per gram Cost: $10k–$50k

Vendors: Not among the commercial products surveyed in the review (Table 3); figures here are illustrative.

Suitable materials: All powders (even bridging, cohesive, electrostatic)

Advantages: Highest accuracy; works with all powder types

Limitations: High cost; requires compressed air supply

docs.title: Gravimetric Feedback Systems
docs.text:
Principle: Real-time weighing on collection vessel; adjusts feeder speed to match target.

Accuracy: ±0.5–1% (depends on scale precision) Speed: 20–60 sec per dose (includes feedback cycles) Cost: $8k–$30k (feeder + scale + controller)

Vendors: Mettler-Toledo (Quantos, 0.001 mg readability, quote only) [72], Chemspeed (GDU) [71]. Performance varies strongly with powder properties; systems often jam or require per-material calibration [18]

Suitable materials: Any powder

Control strategy: Iterative Optimization (Strategy 2) or Real-Time Correction (Strategy 3)

docs.title: 6-DOF Collaborative Robots
docs.text:
Principle: Motorized joints, each with encoders and torque sensors; compute target positions via kinematics.

Accuracy: ±0.03 mm (UR3e) to ±0.5 mm (UFACTORY Lite 6) repeatability [51], [52], [53] Speed: Cycle time 5–30 sec (depends on task) Cost: ~$4,200 (Lite 6) to ~$30,000 (UR3e); 7-DOF cobots ~$30,000–35,000 [51], [53], [54], [55]

Vendors: Universal Robots, UFACTORY, Franka Robotics, Kinova (see Robot Classes)

Suitable for: Object pick-and-place, assembly, inspection

Control strategies: Tactile Retrieval (Strategy 7), Real-Time Correction (Strategy 3)

docs.title: Parallel Gripper
docs.text:
• Cost: $1k–$3k
  • Grip force: 100–1000 N
  • Suitable: Rigid objects, boxes, rigid parts
  • Limitations: Cannot adapt to soft or irregular shapes

docs.title: Vacuum Gripper
docs.text:
• Cost: $500–$2k (suction cup only)
  • Lifting capacity: 1–50 kg (depends on cup area, vacuum pump)
  • Suitable: Flat, smooth, non-porous objects
  • Limitations: Won't work on porous or deformable materials

docs.title: Soft Gripper
docs.text:
• Cost: $2k–$10k
  • Grip force: 1–10 N (gentle)
  • Suitable: Delicate objects (tissue, fruit, fragile electronics)
  • Limitations: Lower speed; may slip on smooth hard objects

docs.title: Electroadhesion Gripper
docs.text:
• Cost: $3k–$10k
  • Lifting capacity: 10–500 g (depends on voltage, material)
  • Suitable: Any material (uses electrostatic force)
  • Advantages: Non-contact; works on glass, foil, ceramics
  • Limitations: Requires conductive gripper pad and target

docs.title: Pick-and-Place Systems (Gantry / SCARA)
docs.text:
Principle: Fast XY(Z) motion; specialized for high-speed discrete part handling.

Accuracy: Gantries ±0.1–0.5 mm; SCARA ±0.010–0.09 mm repeatability [46], [47], [49], [50] Speed: 1–3 sec per pick (very fast) Cost: $599 (desktop CNC gantry) to ~$2,500 (igus drylin); ~$1,400 open-source Jubilee; SCARA ~$10,000 or quote [46], [47], [48], [49], [50]

Vendors: SainSmart, igus, Machine Agency (Jubilee), Precise Automation, Epson

Suitable for: Tablets, pellets, small assemblies (food, pharma, electronics)

Advantages: Faster than 6-DOF robots for planar tasks

docs.title: Commercial Hardware: Cost vs. Accuracy Trade-Off
docs.text:
Illustrative estimates

The cost and accuracy figures on this page are illustrative estimates from the earlier version of this wiki, useful for reasoning about trade-offs. For sourced product accuracies and prices, use Commercial Dispensers (Table 3), Integrated Platforms (Table 4) and Robot Classes (Table 2). Named-product figures below have been aligned with the review.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Automated material handling systems span a wide cost range ($1k–$500k+) with corresponding accuracy ranges (±1%–±20%). This page helps you navigate the trade-off: which system offers the best accuracy for your budget?

docs.title: Sourced view: price versus mechanism (Figure 5)
docs.text: Figure 5. (A) Commercial dispensers and platforms by material class, mechanism and price (hollow markers: quote only; bracketed numbers: references). (B–E) Qualitative 0–10 profiles of four platforms (‘solid handling’: labware transfer). Photographs adapted from Opentrons [15], Chemspeed [71], Hamilton [16] and Eppendorf [75].

docs.title: Pharmaceutical Manufacturing
docs.text:
• Tablet coating: ±0.5% (stringent)
  • API powder dispensing: ±1% (stringent)
  • Liquid fill: ±2% (moderate)
  • Quality control: ±0.1% (very stringent)

Recommended system: Fluidized-bed or gravimetric + feedback, cost $20–50k

docs.title: Chemical Synthesis (Lab Scale)
docs.text:
• Liquid addition: ±2–5% (moderate)
  • Powder reagent: ±5% (loose)
  • Dosing multiple ingredients: ±2% each (moderate)

Recommended system: Syringe pump + gravimetric scale, cost $5–15k

docs.title: Food/Cosmetic Ingredient Dosing
docs.text:
• Texture-critical ingredients: ±1% (stringent)
  • Volume-only ingredients: ±5–10% (loose)
  • Batch-to-batch consistency: ±3% (moderate)

Recommended system: Auger + visual verification, cost $5–10k

docs.title: Robotic Bin Picking
docs.text:
• Position accuracy: ±1–5 mm (moderate, depends on next step)
  • Grasp reliability: 95%+ (behavioral; not % accuracy)
  • Cycle time: < 10 sec (speed critical)

Recommended system: UR3e + parallel gripper, cost $40–50k

docs.title: "I need ±1% accuracy, minimum cost"
docs.text:
Option 1: Gravimetric feedback (Iterative Optimization) - Auger feeder: $5k - Scale (0.01 g resolution): $2k - Controller: $1k - Total: $8k - Time to achieve ±1%: 30 sec per batch (feedback cycles)

Option 2: Manual + scale (Characterize, Then Act) - Manual scoop: $0 - Scale: $2k - Model from experience: $0 - Total: $2k - Time to achieve ±1%: Requires expert, 5 min per batch

Winner: Option 1 if repeatability required; Option 2 if one-off trials

docs.title: "I need 95% grasp reliability, under $50k"
docs.text:
Option 1: UR3e + gripper + force feedback - UR3e robot: ~$30k [51] - Parallel gripper: $3k - Force/torque sensor: $2k - ROS software: Free - Total: ~$35k - Grasp reliability: 92–95% (with real-time correction)

Option 2: UR3e + vision system + gripper - UR3e robot: ~$30k [51] - Camera + lighting: $3k - Parallel gripper: $2k - Vision-based grasping software: $3k - Total: ~$38k - Grasp reliability: 85–90% (vision occlusion limits)

Winner: Option 1 if occlusion is a problem; Option 2 if lighting is good

docs.title: "I want the fastest powder dispensing, cost no object"
docs.text:
Option 1: Fluidized-bed + gravimetric + feedback - Fluidized-bed feeder: $25k - Scale: $3k - PLC controller: $1k - Compressed air: $1k - Total: $30k - Cycle time: 15–20 sec per dose, ±0.5% accuracy

Option 2: Vibratory hopper (open loop, no feedback) - Vibratory feeder: $2k - Calibrated exit orifice: $0.5k - Total: $2.5k - Cycle time: 5 sec per dose, ±10% accuracy

Winner: Option 1 if accuracy matters; Option 2 if speed matters and tolerance is loose

docs.title: ROI Analysis: When Does Higher Cost Pay Off?
Example: Pharmaceutical API Dispensing (1000 doses/month, API cost $500/g)
Scenario A: Low-Cost System ($5k)
docs.text:
Equipment cost: $5k amortized over 24 months = $208/month
Waste from ±5% errors: 50 doses × 5% × $500 = $12,500/month!
Total cost of ownership: $12,708/month
Unacceptable.

docs.title: Scenario B: Mid-Cost System ($15k)
docs.text:
Equipment cost: $15k amortized = $625/month
Waste from ±1% errors: 50 doses × 1% × $500 = $2,500/month
Total cost of ownership: $3,125/month
Acceptable.

docs.title: Scenario C: High-Cost System ($30k)
docs.text:
Equipment cost: $30k amortized = $1,250/month
Waste from ±0.5% errors: 50 doses × 0.5% × $500 = $1,250/month
Total cost of ownership: $2,500/month
Best option.

Lesson: For high-value materials (API, rare reagents), investing in ±0.5% accuracy system pays for itself in waste reduction.

docs.text:
Systems where no competitor offers better accuracy for lower cost:

System Accuracy Cost Use Case Throughput Manual + scale ±2–5% $1k One-off trials Very slow Auger + manual ±5% $3k Training material Slow Auger + feedback ±1–2% $10k Production low-viscosity Medium Fluidized-bed ±0.5% $25k Production high-value Medium UR3e + gripper ±0.03 mm ~$33k Object handling Medium–fast Tecan Fluent 1080 CV ≤3% at 10 µL, ≤0.5% at 100 µL [77] $32,995–75,000 Multi-channel liquid Very fast

docs.title: Hidden Costs (Often Forgotten)
docs.text:
• Training: $2k–$10k for operator certification
  • Validation: $5k–$20k for GMP/FDA compliance (pharma)
  • Maintenance: $1k–$5k/year for spare parts, calibration
  • Integration: $5k–$50k for software, hooking up to existing systems
  • Downtime: Lost productivity if equipment breaks (non-negotiable)
  • Calibration standards: $1k–$5k for reference materials
  • Compressed air (if needed): $200–$500/month supply cost

docs.title: Recommendation: Decision Tree
docs.text:
START
├─ Material type?
│  ├─ Liquid
│  │  ├─ Accuracy need ±5% or worse?
│  │  │  └─ → Manual pipette ($1k) or syringe pump ($5k)
│  │  └─ Accuracy need ±1–2%?
│  │     ├─ Volume < 100 mL?
│  │     │  └─ → Peristaltic or syringe pump ($5–10k)
│  │     └─ Volume > 100 mL?
│  │        └─ → Gravimetric scale + pump ($10–20k)
│  │
│  ├─ Powder
│  │  ├─ Accuracy need ±10% or worse?
│  │  │  └─ → Vibratory hopper ($2k)
│  │  ├─ Accuracy need ±2–5%?
│  │  │  └─ → Auger ± feedback ($8–15k)

docs.title: Commercial Dispensers by Material Class
docs.text:
Step 3 · Buy: What can be bought?

This page summarizes Section 4 and Table 3 of the review. All accuracy and price figures come from the V3 manuscript and its cited sources. Prices come from list prices, distributor listings, secondary-market sales or itemized quotes, and are marked as such. Older illustrative estimates are kept on By Yield Stress & Cost.

Knowing how each ingredient should be dispensed and moved only helps if hardware can do it. That raises a question that applies to all three material classes: which commercial option gives acceptable accuracy for a given material, and at what cost?

The market is uneven on both counts:

  • Accuracy. Liquid-handling vendors almost always publish quantified accuracy and precision, often per ISO 8655. Powder and paste dispensing vendors often describe their systems only qualitatively.
  • Price. Prices are rarely public. Apart from Opentrons, none of the integrated platforms in the review publishes a list price.

The market is therefore least transparent where formulation handling is hardest, and quote-only pricing is itself a barrier for SDL groups trying to budget a hardware stack.

docs.title: Liquids
docs.text:
Liquids have the most mature and transparent market:

  • Air-displacement pipettes range from the Rainin E4 XLS+ (±0.8%, $191–350) to the Eppendorf Xplorer (~±0.6%, ~$1,300). Paying more buys throughput and integration more than accuracy.
  • Positive-displacement pipettes accept a wider accuracy band (Gilson MICROMAN E, ±3–8%) in exchange for a low price (~$525).
  • Syringe pumps: Hamilton's PSD/4 gets back to ±1% at a low OEM price.
  • Precision peristaltic pumps (Watson-Marlow Qdos 20, ±1%; Masterflex L/S) cost $4,000–9,000.

docs.title: Semi-solids
docs.text:
Semi-solid dispensing splits into two segments:

  • Bioprinting: list prices but unquantified accuracy. CELLINK printheads cost $2,500–3,190. The Allevi 2 costs $15,000 and reports only motion-stage precision.
  • Industrial: tight accuracy but quote-only pricing. The ViscoTec preeflow eco-PEN300 is rated ±1%.

Integrated formulation workstations such as the Chemspeed FLEX FORMAX combine liquid, viscous-liquid and powder dosing in one enclosure, but are also sold only by quote [152].

docs.title: Powders
docs.text:
Powders reverse the liquid market. Reported resolution is excellent: ±10 µg for the Chemspeed SWILE and 0.001 mg readability for the Quantos. But Coperion K-Tron, Chemspeed SWILE/GDU and Mettler-Toledo Quantos systems are all sold only by quote. Secondary-market components, such as $9,800 for a bare Coperion micro-feeder, are the only price signal.

Key finding

Across all three material classes, price follows mechanism class and ecosystem rather than accuracy.

docs.title: Integrated Platforms
docs.text:
Step 3 · Buy: What can be bought?

This page summarizes Section 4.2 and Table 4 of the review.

An SDL usually buys an integrated platform rather than a bare mechanism. The eight platforms in Table 4 vary in price by more than an order of magnitude, without a comparable spread in accuracy.

  • Opentrons OT-2/Flex. The open-source option, and the only one with a list price ($15,950–26,400). Its accuracy is unusually well documented and depends strongly on volume: ±15% at 1 µL, ±0.6% at 300 µL.
  • Hamilton Microlab STAR, Eppendorf epMotion 5075, Tecan Fluent, Beckman Coulter Biomek i7 and Agilent Bravo. Where they publish accuracy, it is broadly comparable and below 5%. Their price differences come from throughput, deck configuration and software ecosystem.
  • Two non-contact platforms for very-low-volume screening. The pressure-driven Dispendix I.DOT handles 8 nL–30 µL, with <5% error above 100 nL. The acoustic Beckman Coulter Echo 525 handles 25 nL–5 µL, with <10% accuracy and <8% precision. Neither has a public price.

docs.title: Generalist versus specialist
docs.text:
Figure 5. (A) Commercial dispensers and platforms by material class, mechanism and price (hollow markers: quote only; bracketed numbers: references). (B–E) Qualitative 0–10 profiles of four platforms (‘solid handling’: labware transfer). Photographs adapted from Opentrons [15], Chemspeed [71], Hamilton [16] and Eppendorf [75].

Placed on one price axis, the products fall into three patterns:

  • List-priced products cluster in liquid handling.
  • Most paste and powder dispensers are sold only by quote.
  • Each product serves one material class through one mechanism.

The Opentrons Flex and the Hamilton Microlab STAR go furthest beyond a single class. Each is sold with an optional gripper arm that moves labware as well as liquid. Even as an add-on, this generalist capability shows commercially that the direction argued in the review is feasible: platforms that recognize which part of the material spectrum they are working in and switch tools to match.

The review rates four platforms on nine criteria to make the generalist-versus-specialist trade-off explicit (Fig. 5B–E):

  • accuracy
  • price
  • liquid versatility
  • solid handling (labware transfer)
  • powder handling
  • throughput
  • programming simplicity
  • deck capacity and footprint
  • maintenance cost

Where the catalog ends, researchers take over: see Retrofits Beyond Factory Spec.

See also: Commercial Dispensers · Robot Classes

docs.title: Retrofits Beyond Factory Specification
docs.text:
Step 4 · Extend: How to go beyond the catalog?

Summarizes Section 5 (Customizing Platforms Beyond Their Factory Specification) and Table 5 of the review.

The optional gripper arms on the Opentrons Flex and the Hamilton Microlab STAR are the manufacturer-approved route to generalization. A larger body of work gets there without the vendor. Researchers keep a platform's gantry, deck and control loop, then swap its end-effector, add a sensor or replace its control software to unlock a capability the manufacturer never sold.

The literature scenarios ask how a material should be handled. This work asks a different question: which layer of a platform you already own should you modify (mechanical, sensing or software) so that one machine can cover more steps of a formulation workflow? Table 5 groups ten studies by that layer. Three of them also appear among the liquid-handling scenarios; seven are new here.

docs.title: 1. Replace the end-effector
docs.text:
The most direct retrofit keeps the motion system and replaces the end-effector (Table 5, rows 3–7). There are two threads.

Reuse the robot's own actuator. Councill et al. turn the stepper motor of the now-discontinued Opentrons OT-1 into a nanoliter syringe pump [82]. Axtell et al. show that the same retrofit, with valves added, also works as an LC-MS autosampler [83].

Platform-agnostic tools. Yoshikawa et al.'s open-hardware digital pipette [84] and Zwirnmann et al.'s gripper fingers, designed from a container-shape taxonomy [85], fit any compatible arm. They give up deep integration in exchange for reuse across a fleet.

docs.title: 2. Use the tool changer as a sensor mount
docs.text: A second family uses the tool-change mechanism, built for pipette tips, to mount a different tool. Nazeri et al. [86] and del Olmo Lianes et al. [87] both mount a camera on an Opentrons OT-2: the first to monitor dispensing, the second to pick colonies. What is new is not the commodity camera but the idea of treating a consumables interface as a general-purpose mount.

docs.title: 3. Replace the control software
docs.text:
A third family works at the software layer. Wierenga et al.'s PyLabRobot [88] replaces proprietary control software with one hardware-agnostic Python interface for Opentrons, Hamilton and Tecan platforms. It exposes moves that are physically possible but that vendor firmware never programmed, such as an 8-channel head servicing two microplates in one motion.

Layers like this underpin every other customization. A robot cannot act on a new sensor through firmware that refuses non-standard commands, and a formulation workflow cannot be orchestrated across instruments that refuse a common interface. See also Orchestration.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Together, these retrofits can turn a $15,000–30,000 liquid handler into a nanoliter dispenser, an autosampler, a colony picker or an imaging station. The cost is a few hundred dollars in printed parts plus a workaround in the control layer. They are a lower-cost counterpart to the new-hardware scenarios E–H in Figure 3, and they turn single-purpose robots into the multi-function platforms formulation SDLs need.

Every new capability is a new failure mode

Proving a retrofit on the physical cell is slow and risky, which is the motivation for rehearsing it first in simulation and digital twins.

See also: Physical Reinvention · Integrated Platforms

docs.title: Dispensing by Material Class
docs.text:
Step 1 · Dose: How is each ingredient dosed?

This page summarizes Section 2 (Material Handling) of the review. The 20 studies it draws on are listed on the Literature Scenarios page, and the governing properties are covered in Material Properties.

How hard a material is to handle depends on how it behaves. Formulation materials run along a continuum: low-viscosity Newtonian liquids, then viscous liquids, then yield-stress gels and pastes, then powders and granular solids. Each flows and deforms differently, so each needs different handling principles [13], [14]. Viscosity and rheology govern liquids and semi-solids, while flowability and cohesion govern powders.

The review groups materials by how they are handled rather than by strict physical state:

  • Liquids flow freely under gravity and can be pipetted or pumped.
  • Semi-solids have a yield stress, or a viscosity high enough that they must be extruded.
  • Powders are particulate solids.

Newtonian and non-Newtonian behavior can occur in both fluid classes.

Each class fails in its own way:

  • Viscous liquids and gels defeat air-displacement pipettes. The pipette has to wait for the air cushion to equilibrate, and material clings to the tip.
  • Semi-solids that melt or set clog nozzles or need inline heating.
  • Powders jam dosing heads and need calibration for each material.
  • Sticky or colored materials raise cross-contamination and cleaning concerns.

docs.title: Liquids
docs.text:
Liquid Fig. 3A–H

Liquids are the most mature handling problem. For that reason they show most clearly where vendor defaults stop working and where sensing and feedback have to take over. Viscosity dominates automated liquid dispensing because it sets pressure losses, flow stability, droplet formation and the volumetric accuracy that can be reached [14], [19], [20]. Most laboratory liquids are Newtonian, so a single measured viscosity is usually enough to pick a technology.

Three mechanisms cover nearly the whole range:

  • Air-displacement pipetting. A piston moves an air cushion. This is the commercial default for low and medium viscosities [21].
  • Positive-displacement pipetting. The piston touches the liquid. It is insensitive to viscosity but needs a dedicated syringe.
  • Peristaltic pumping. Rollers squeeze a tube. It tolerates the widest range of liquids.

Volatility also matters. Volatile solvents evaporate into the air cushion of an air-displacement pipette and drip from the tip. They are usually handled by pre-wetting tips, reverse pipetting or positive displacement.

Standard air-displacement robots from Opentrons, Tecan and Hamilton handle water-like liquids with <1% error at high speed, and their documented range is wider than that label suggests. An Opentrons application note by Kanase and Watson [21] reports that unmodified GEN2 pipettes dispense up to 99% glycerol (≈900–1400 cP). Losses stay below 0.9% on the P20 and below 0.2% on the P300/P1000, provided aspiration and dispensing are slowed, settling delays are added and the tip is withdrawn more slowly. The vendor-documented ceiling therefore sits near 1,000–1,400 cP. It exists only as a lookup table of hand-tuned settings for a few named liquids: glycerol dilutions, PEG 8000, hand sanitizer, Tween 20 and engine oil.

Eight literature scenarios go beyond this envelope (Fig. 3A–H). They differ in how they get past the lookup table:

  • Measure the viscosity directly:
    • Mass-flow viscometry reaches 5000 cP [22].
    • Proxy viscometry on a standard Opentrons platform covers 20–20,000 cP [23].
  • Retune the pipetting: Bayesian optimization under gravimetric feedback reaches <5% error at 1275 cP [11].
  • Change the hardware:
    • A self-focusing acoustic pipet ejects picoliter droplets [24].
    • An acoustofluidic end-effector mixes liquids 10⁶× more viscous than water [25].
    • Containerless pendant-drop handling serves synchrotron X-ray measurement [26].
    • A soft peristaltic pump conveys liquid by compressing a soft actuator [27].
    • A robot infers viscosity from its own filmed flow with 88% accuracy, against 32% for human estimates [28].

For a formulation SDL, the lesson is that viscous ingredients do not have to be diluted or excluded. Measured viscosity, closed-loop gravimetric tuning and new dispensing hardware together extend automated liquid handling to ingredients outside the vendor's tables. Studies that modify the stock liquid handler itself are covered in Retrofits.

docs.title: Semi-solids: pastes, gels and slurries
docs.text:
Semi-solid Fig. 3I–L

Semi-solids add shear-rate dependence and a yield stress to the liquid problem. The task shifts from tuning a flow rate to sensing how a material deforms. These are also the ingredients that most often define a formulated product, from creams and pastes to inks, slurries and the polymer solutions used to form porous mats [29].

Pastes, gels, slurries and bio-inks are typically shear-thinning, occasionally shear-thickening, and may have a yield stress below which they behave as solids. The actuator therefore has to supply enough force or shear to start the flow, and the yield stress has to be measured and compensated for consistent dispensing [30]. Industry characterizes these materials at two representative shear rates rather than sampling the full flow curve [19]: a low rate for storage and gentle handling, and a high rate for extrusion and spraying.

Semi-solids are generally moved by extrusion:

  • Syringe-based: precise, but needs a dedicated piston.
  • Air-pressure-driven: gentler on shear-sensitive bio-inks, but slower to respond.
  • Screw-based: an auger decouples flow from pressure, which suits viscous or particle-laden pastes.

The same three mechanisms scale up to industrial adhesive and sealant dispensing.

Four scenarios (Fig. 3I–L) show that a formulation SDL can infer a paste's rheology from how it responds to stirring, poking or extrusion, without a separate rheometer:

  • Stirring forces: viscosity is estimated from stirring forces [31].
  • Poking with a differentiable-physics twin: yield stress, modulus and friction are identified [32].
  • Vision during bioprinting: over- and under-extrusion are corrected within about 10 s [33].
  • Feedforward prediction: droplet size is predicted from bio-ink viscosity [34].

These studies rely more on estimation and modeling than the liquid studies do. A paste's rheology depends on its shear history, so a single viscosity reading cannot capture it. The open goal is to build in such sensing and feedback without deriving a new policy for every formulation.

docs.title: Powders and granular materials
docs.text:
Powder Fig. 3M–T

Powders replace continuous flow with friction and cohesion at the particle scale. As a result, acquiring a dose is the step most likely to fail, not delivering it. Powder flow depends on particle size, shape, density, cohesion and surface interactions, and is summarized by the angle of repose and the Hausner ratio. Cohesive powders bridge (arch) or rat-hole in hoppers, which makes dosing unpredictable. Tribocharging [35] and humidity cause wall adhesion and variable packing, so the same equipment rarely dispenses different powders equally well [12].

The right mechanism depends strongly on particle size, which ranges from cohesive sub-100 µm fines to coarse granules that flow almost like liquids:

  • Fine powders can be conveyed pneumatically.
  • Granules can be dosed volumetrically through rotary valves.
  • Discrete units such as tablets can be picked and placed under vacuum.

At laboratory scale, three mechanisms dominate:

  • Auger or screw feeders: continuous and volumetric.
  • Vacuum-assisted heads: milligram doses through a narrow orifice.
  • Vibratory hoppers: struggle with sticky or charged powders.

Commercial systems such as the Chemspeed Gravimetric Dispensing Unit (GDU) and the Mettler-Toledo Quantos perform very differently depending on powder properties, and often jam or need per-material calibration [18]. The stakes are high. Autonomous solid-state synthesis [4] and a self-driving pharmaceutical tableting line [36] both start every experiment with automated powder dosing, so the choice and calibration of the dosing mechanism directly limit what these platforms can make.

Eight scenarios go beyond fixed dispensers (Fig. 3M–T):

  • Tuned vacuum transfer: ≤0.1% RSD milligram transfers [37].
  • Vision-guided deep-RL scooping: ~1.93 mg error across seven powders [12].
  • Simulation-trained scooping: transfers to unseen powders [38].
  • Simulators calibrated from flowability: extend to cohesive, unseen powders [39].
  • Soft funnel-shaped hand: doses to ±2 mg [40].
  • Chainable RL policies from a differentiable granular simulator [41].
  • Bayesian optimization with computer-vision foam assessment [42].
  • Tactile retrieval of buried objects [43].

Related work coordinates excavation and deposition of cohesive granular media [44], and Lo et al.'s low-cost Frugal Twin fills and melts wax powder into candles [45].

For a formulation SDL, the powder step is where generalization is hardest, because every new powder changes flowability. The methods that transfer best are those that sense or simulate the powder rather than assume its behavior. Once the ingredients are dosed, the premix itself becomes an object that has to be moved: see Object Handling.

docs.title: Literature Scenarios (Figure 3)
docs.text:
Step 1 · Dose

The review condenses recent work on adaptive material handling into 20 literature scenarios, each named after its sense–act sequence: liquids (A–H), semi-solids (I–L), and powders and granular media (M–T). The scenarios cover different scales and were validated on different materials. They illustrate complementary strategies (measure, retune or redesign) and are not directly comparable benchmarks.

docs.title: Liquids (A–H)
docs.text:
Liquid

All eight liquid scenarios run into the same limit: there is no measurement of how an unfamiliar liquid will behave. They cover picoliter to milliliter volumes.

  • A · focus → eject → dispense. Zhang et al.'s self-focusing acoustic pipet ejects picoliter droplets without contact [24].
  • B · flow → measure → infer. Deshmukh et al.'s mass-flow viscometry measures viscosity directly, up to 5000 cP [22].
  • C · dispense → measure → generalize. Proxy viscometry on a standard Opentrons platform covers 20–20,000 cP [23].
  • D · dispense → weigh → optimize. Bayesian-optimized pipetting under gravimetric feedback replaces the vendor's per-liquid table and reaches <5% error at 1275 cP [11].
  • E · couple → vibrate → mix. Durrer et al.'s acoustofluidic end-effector mixes liquids 10⁶× more viscous than water [25].
  • F · suspend → isolate → measure. Ozgulbas et al.'s containerless pendant-drop handling supports synchrotron X-ray measurement [26].
  • G · actuate → compress → convey. Xu et al.'s soft peristaltic pump [27].
  • H · perturb → watch → infer. Walker et al.'s robot infers viscosity from video of the flow it induces, using a convolutional neural network. It is right 88% of the time, against 32% for human estimates [28]. The scenario asks whether viscosity needs to be known at all.

docs.title: Semi-solids (I–L)
docs.text:
Semi-solid

  • I · sense → estimate → act. Luo et al.'s pancake-batter robot estimates viscosity from stirring forces, using a force/torque sensor and a camera, and plans a pouring trajectory with a small neural network. It remains calibrated to one material [31].
  • J · poke → simulate → identify. Yang et al. poke an unknown paste with an end-effector that has a camera in hand. A differentiable-physics twin recovers the paste's yield stress, modulus and friction coefficient, and the method generalizes across materials [32].
  • K · watch → detect → correct. Kelly et al. close the loop on extrusion bioprinting, correcting over- and under-extrusion from computer vision within about 10 s [33].
  • L · measure → predict → print. Shin et al. predict droplet size and volume from bio-ink viscosity and print parameters before printing, the feedforward counterpart of K [34].

docs.title: Powders and granular media (M–T)
docs.text:
Powder / granular

  • M · draw → tune → dose. Fermier et al. tuned vacuum flow and orifice size to reach ≤0.1% RSD on milligram transfers, for one powder and offline [37].
  • N · scoop → verify → pour. Radulov et al. use vision-guided deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to scoop, correct the volume in real time and reach ~1.93 mg error across seven powders [12].
  • O · scoop → dump → transfer. Kadokawa et al. train a policy entirely in simulation that transfers to unseen powders without retuning [38].
  • P · measure → calibrate → dispense. A simulator is calibrated from measured flowability and generalizes to cohesive, unseen powders [39].
  • Q · funnel → valve → trickle. Takahashi et al.'s soft funnel-shaped hand trickles milligram doses through a valve to ±2 mg [40].
  • R · scoop → transport → pour. Three chainable RL policies are bootstrapped from Wei et al.'s differentiable granular simulator [41].
  • S · pour → mix → assess. Bayesian optimization combined with computer-vision foam assessment reconstitutes a powdered beverage [42]. This is a complete formulate-and-evaluate loop in miniature.
  • T · probe → feel → retrieve. Xu et al. retrieve an object of unknown shape buried in granular media using tactile feedback alone [43].

docs.title: Mapping scenarios to the recurring strategies
docs.text:
The seven recurring strategies of this wiki group the same studies by control philosophy. Some scenarios fit more than one strategy.

Strategy Scenarios Characterize, then act B [22], C [23], I [31], P [39] Iterative optimization D [11], M [37], S [42] Real-time correction K [33], N [12] Feedforward prediction H [28], L [34] Simulation-based generalization J [32], O [38], P [39], R [41] Physical reinvention A [24], E [25], F [26], G [27], Q [40] Tactile retrieval T [43]

docs.title: Material Properties Governing Handling Strategies
docs.text:
Updated to manuscript V3

The review groups formulation materials by how they are handled: liquids (pipetted or pumped), semi-solids (yield stress or viscosity high enough to require extrusion) and powders (particulate solids) [13], [14]. Its Table 1, reproduced on Dispensing by Material Class, gives the working ranges used throughout this wiki: low-viscosity liquids 1–20 cP, medium 20–500 cP, high 500–100,000 cP; gels with yield stress ~10–500 Pa; pastes ~100–10,000 Pa, often thixotropic; powders from free-flowing (Hausner ratio ~1.00–1.11) to very cohesive (>1.4), with angles of repose from ~25° to >66°. Industry characterizes semi-solids at two representative shear rates (low, ~1–10 s⁻¹, and high, ~100–1000 s⁻¹) rather than the full flow curve [19]; tribocharging [35] and humidity drive wall adhesion in powders.

Figure 2. Material properties and handling mechanisms: (A) liquids to pastes and (B) powders by cohesion; (C, E, G) selection charts and (D, F, H) mechanisms for liquids, semi-solids and powders. Product photographs adapted from Opentrons [15], Hamilton [16], Nordson EFD [17] and XQ Instruments; powder dispensers are compared in [18].

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The key physical properties of liquids, semi-solids, and powders determine which automated handling strategy is most appropriate. Materials span a continuum from low-viscosity Newtonian liquids to highly viscous pastes, yield-stress fluids, powders, and solid dosage forms.

docs.title: Viscosity and Flow Behavior
docs.text:
Viscosity is the dominant parameter governing automated liquid dispensing because it directly influences: - Pressure losses - Flow stability - Droplet formation - Achievable volumetric accuracy

Newtonian fluids (constant viscosity) are easier to pump and dispense. Examples: water (~1 cP), glycerol (~1500 cP).

Non-Newtonian fluids exhibit viscosity that changes with shear rate: - Shear-thinning materials become less viscous at high shear (e.g., polymer solutions, food sauces) - Shear-thickening materials harden under stress (rare in labs) - Yield-stress (Bingham) fluids behave like solids until applied stress exceeds their yield point (e.g., certain gels, pastes)

docs.title: Yield Stress
docs.text:
Materials with yield stress require sufficient force or shear to initiate flow. Handling these requires: - Pumps or robotic actuators that provide enough force - Feedback loops to detect when flow starts - Special dispensing strategies (sense→estimate→act; watch→detect→correct)

Standard air-displacement pipettes typically fail above ~100 cP viscosity.

docs.title: Semi-Solids and Gels
docs.text:
Semi-solid materials (pastes, adhesives, bio-inks) often combine: - Viscous behavior at rest (storage) - Elastic behavior under stress (recovers shape) - Yield stress below which they behave like a solid

Industry characterizes them at two representative shear rates: - Low shear (storage, gentle handling) - High shear (extrusion, spraying)

Rather than sampling the full flow curve.

docs.title: Powder Properties
docs.text: Powder handling depends on multiple interrelated properties:

docs.title: Flowability Metrics
docs.text:
• Angle of repose — the angle at which a powder forms a stable pile
  • Hausner ratio — ratio of tapped to poured bulk density
  • These reflect interparticle friction and cohesion

docs.title: Particle Size Distribution
docs.text:
• Very fine powders (dust-like, < 100 µm) may require fluidized or vacuum-assisted feeding
  • Coarse granules may not compact well and flow more readily
  • Cohesive fines can agglomerate or bridge, making dosing unpredictable

docs.title: Surface Interactions
docs.text:
• Electrostatic charge (tribocharging) causes powders to cling to surfaces
  • Moisture sensitivity — hygroscopic powders absorb water, changing flowability
  • Surface area affects interparticle forces

docs.title: Common Failure Modes
docs.text:
• Bridging (arch formation) — powder gets stuck in the hopper
  • Rat-holing (funnel flow) — flow channels through the powder, leaving unmixed material
  • Caking — compaction due to moisture or pressure

docs.title: The Material Spectrum: From Liquids to Solids
docs.text:
Updated to manuscript V3

In the review the spectrum is organized by handling class (liquids, semi-solids, powders and discrete objects) rather than by a single yield-stress axis, and each class is mapped onto dispensing technologies with typical accuracy and throughput (Table 1, on Dispensing by Material Class). The yield-stress ranges below are the earlier wiki's illustrative organizing axis; for the review's sourced ranges, see Table 1. Discrete objects (vials, premix containers, lids) are treated in Object Handling.

docs.title: Yield Stress as the Organizing Axis
docs.text:
Materials encountered in autonomous formulation laboratories span a continuum based on yield stress — the minimum stress required for flow:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  10⁰ Pa         10² Pa         10⁴ Pa         10⁶ Pa         10⁹ Pa
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
│  LIQUIDS      SEMI-SOLIDS      POWDERS       SOLIDS
│  (flow)       (yield-stress)   (granular)    (rigid)
│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Lower yield stress → higher mobility → continuous flow Higher yield stress → lower mobility → discrete manipulation

docs.title: Liquids (Yield Stress ~10⁰ – 10² Pa)
docs.text:
Discrete Dispensing: - Air-displacement pipettes (standard for < 100 cP) - Positive-displacement syringes - Syringe pumps

Continuous Dispensing: - Peristaltic pumps - Gear pumps

Contactless: - Acoustic droplet ejection - Piezoelectric dispensers

Dominant Strategy: Characterize (measure viscosity) → Act

docs.title: Semi-Solids & Gels (Yield Stress ~10² – 10⁵ Pa)
docs.text:
Extrusion-Based: - Syringe-based extrusion (motor drives plunger) - Air pressure-driven (gentler on shear-sensitive bio-inks) - Screw/auger extrusion (decouples flow from pressure)

Progressive Cavity Pumps: For consistent output despite yield stress

Dominant Strategies: - Real-time correction (watch→detect→correct) - Iterative optimization (dispense→weigh→optimize) - Feedforward prediction (measure→predict→print)

docs.title: Powders (Yield Stress ~10⁴ – 10⁶ Pa, Granular)
docs.text:
Feeding Methods: - Auger/screw feeders (volumetric control) - Vacuum-assisted dosing (suction through orifice) - Vibratory hoppers (struggles with sticky/charged powders)

Feedback: - Gravimetric (weigh continuously or at endpoints) - Vision (estimate fill height in scoops) - Tactile (touch-based retrieval)

Dominant Strategies: - Simulation-based generalization (train in sim, apply to unseen powders) - Real-time correction (scoop→verify→pour) - Iterative optimization (measure→calibrate→dispense)

docs.title: Solids (Yield Stress ~10⁶ – 10⁹ Pa)
docs.text:
Discrete Object Handling: - 6-DOF robotic arms (UR3e, Franka, Kinova) - SCARA robots (higher precision) - Cartesian/gantry systems (lower cost)

End-Effectors: - Vacuum grippers - Parallel grippers - Soft/compliant grippers - Vision-guided pick-and-place

Dominant Strategy: Tactile retrieval (probe→feel→retrieve)

docs.title: The Spectrum in Practice
docs.text:
The yield-stress spectrum determines not only which mechanism to use, but also which strategy to employ:

Yield Stress (Pa) Material Handling Class Primary Mechanism Primary Strategy Typical Accuracy 10⁰ – 10¹ Water, solvents Liquid Pipette/pump Characterize Excellent (< 1%) 10¹ – 10² Honey, oil Liquid Syringe/peristaltic Characterize or iterate High 10² – 10³ Thick paste, gel Semi-solid Screw extrusion Real-time correction Moderate 10³ – 10⁵ Yield-stress paste Semi-solid Air-pressure extrusion Watch→detect→correct Moderate 10⁴ – 10⁶ Powder (free-flowing) Granular Auger/vibration Simulation generation Variable 10⁶ – 10⁸ Powder (cohesive) Granular Gravimetric + vision Real-time correction Good (±1 mg) 10⁸ – 10⁹ Tablet, pellet Solid Pick-and-place Tactile retrieval Excellent

docs.title: Key Insight: Strategies Recur Across Materials
docs.text:
While each material class presents distinct physical challenges (viscosity, flow, cohesion), the underlying control strategies are remarkably similar:

  • Both high-viscosity liquids and pastes benefit from real-time correction
  • Both powders and semi-solids use simulation-based generalization
  • All classes can employ iterative optimization when feedback sensors are available

This strategy-level view reveals that future autonomous labs should:

  1. Identify material properties (yield stress, viscosity, flowability) on the fly
  2. Select the appropriate strategy (characterize, optimize, correct, predict, simulate, reinvent, or retrieve)
  3. Apply the strategy using a shared sensing and control infrastructure
  4. Switch strategies as materials change, without re-engineering the entire system

docs.title: Robot Classes for Object Handling
docs.text:
Step 2 · Move: How do containers move?

Summarizes Section 3 (Object Handling in Formulation SDLs) and Table 2 of the review.

Material handling moves matter. Object handling moves the vessels and tools that hold or dispense it. In a formulation SDL, a robot has to:

  • carry the premix container from the dispensing station to a planetary or overhead mixer;
  • open and close instrument lids;
  • bring a dispensing tool to a container, or a container to a fixed dispenser;
  • cap and uncap vials;
  • load samples into characterization instruments.

These are rigid objects of known geometry, so the problem is one of reach, repeatability, payload and integration, not rheology. Even so, object handling gates every step of the formulation. A dose can only go into a container that is in the right place, and a premix can only be mixed once it reaches the mixer.

Figure 4. Robot classes for object handling, ordered by axes, reach and cost: (A) Cartesian gantry, (B) SCARA, (C) 6-DOF arm, (D) 7-DOF or dual-arm cobot and (E) mobile manipulator; (F) repeatability versus price (Table 2).

docs.title: The five robot classes
docs.text: Object handling Containers, lids, tools and vials

docs.title: Cartesian gantries
docs.text:
A Cartesian gantry moves a tool along orthogonal linear axes over a fixed deck. Gantries are the cheapest and simplest robots to program. Examples:

  • A desktop Genmitsu 4040-PRO CNC frame costs $599 and accepts a gripper or dispensing tool. The vendor quotes ±0.1 mm running accuracy for the series [46].
  • The igus drylin XYZ gantry reaches 0.3–0.5 mm repeatability for under $2,500 [47].
  • The open-source Jubilee platform costs about $1,400 in parts and can swap between a gripper and a pipette [48].

All of them are confined to their frame and can only move objects in-plane and vertically.

docs.title: SCARA lab-automation robots
docs.text: A SCARA robot rides a vertical elevator axis while two revolute links rotate in the horizontal plane. This gives fast, stiff transfers between stations at different heights. The Precise Automation PF400 [49] is common in laboratory automation for tube and plate handling and repeats to ±0.09 mm. The Epson RS3 [50] repeats to ±0.010 mm. Neither can tilt a container or reach into an instrument from the side.

docs.title: 6-DOF articulated arms
docs.text: Six-degree-of-freedom arms can orient the gripper freely. They can open a hinged mixer lid, insert a premix container or tilt a vessel to pour. Prices vary almost tenfold, from the Universal Robots UR3e (±0.03 mm, about $30,000) [51] to the UFACTORY xArm 6 (±0.1 mm, $9,500) [52] and Lite 6 (±0.5 mm, about $4,200) [53]. Arms can also operate equipment designed for people, such as pressing buttons, turning knobs and opening doors, so an SDL can use unmodified benchtop instruments.

docs.title: 7-DOF and dual-arm collaborative robots
docs.text: Seven-degree-of-freedom and dual-arm cobots add redundancy for working around clutter, and a second hand for tasks such as uncapping. Examples are the Franka Research 3 [54], the Kinova Gen3 [55] and the dual-arm robot in Lunt et al.'s solid-state workflow [56].

docs.title: Mobile manipulators
docs.text: A mobile manipulator mounts an arm on an autonomous base, so it can carry samples between stations spread across a laboratory. Examples are the mobile robotic chemist [3], built on a KUKA KMR iiwa, and the synthesis workflow of Dai et al. [57]. The arm repeats to about ±0.1 mm, but the base only relocates to within a few millimeters: about ±5 mm for the KMR iiwa, which sells for about $42,000 on the reseller market [58]. Each docking is therefore usually followed by local re-referencing, such as touching or imaging a fiducial, before the arm grasps [3].

docs.title: End-effectors
docs.text:
In every class, the end-effector matters as much as the arm:

  • Parallel-jaw grippers with container-specific fingers suit vials and premix containers.
  • Vacuum cups suit plates and lids.
  • Tool changers let one arm switch between grippers, pipettes and dispensers.
  • Compliant fingers designed from a container-shape taxonomy let one gripper handle many vessel shapes [85].

docs.title: Table 2: Repeatability and price
docs.text:
Robot class Brand Model Repeatability Price Ref Cartesian gantry pick-and-place SainSmart Genmitsu 4040-PRO CNC ±0.1 mm running accuracy* $599 [46] igus drylin XYZ Gantry 0.3–0.5 mm $2,461 [47] Machine Agency Jubilee (tool-changing) + CNC (gantry) – ~$1,400 [48] SCARA lab-automation robot Precise Automation PreciseFlex PF400 ±0.09 mm Quote [49] Epson RS3 SCARA ±0.010 mm ~$10,000 [50] 6-DOF articulated arm Universal Robots UR3e ±0.03 mm ~$30,000 [51] UFACTORY xArm 6 ±0.1 mm $9,500 [52] UFACTORY Lite 6 ±0.5 mm ~$4,200 [53] 7-DOF collaborative arm Franka Robotics Franka Research 3 <±0.1 mm ~$30,000 [54] Kinova Gen3 ~±0.1 mm ~$35,000 [55] Mobile manipulator KUKA KMR iiwa ±0.1 mm arm; ~±5 mm base positioning ~$42,000 (reseller) [3], [58]

docs.title: Choosing a class
docs.text:
The choice depends on the task, not the material:

If... Choose All stations share one deck Cartesian gantry Throughput and repeatability dominate SCARA Containers must be tilted, inserted or manipulated around instrument geometry (e.g. loading a premix into a mixer) 6-DOF articulated arm Work is cluttered or needs a second hand (e.g. uncapping) 7-DOF or dual-arm cobot Stations cannot be co-located Mobile manipulator

Repeatability and price are only loosely linked (Fig. 4F). Price follows mechanism class, payload and build effort, and the cheapest credible option, an open-source gantry, is not a commercial product at all. The grippers and tool changers on these robots also carry dispensing tools to containers. Object handling is therefore the layer through which every dispensing method on the Dispensing by Material Class page is deployed.

Next: what a formulation SDL can simply buy, in Commercial Dispensers and Integrated Platforms.

docs.title: System Architecture & Orchestration
docs.text:
Step 6 · Orchestrate: How do devices run as one?

This page summarizes Sections 7.1 and 7.3 of the review. The comparison of eight open-source systems (Section 7.2 and Supplementary Table S1) is on Open-Source Orchestration Software.

Dispensers, robots, retrofits and a digital twin only become a self-driving laboratory when software runs them as one system. In a formulation SDL, that software has to run dispensing, transfer, mixing and characterization devices in sequence as a single experiment. Tools are swapped, containers move and ingredients are used up, so the software also has to track:

  • what is mounted where;
  • which container holds which premix;
  • how much material remains.

The review calls this layer orchestration software.

Figure 8. Architecture of a formulation SDL: (A) execution and equipment hierarchies, (B) functional layers of orchestration software and (C) functions provided by eight open-source systems (details in Supplementary Table S1).

docs.title: Terms: two hierarchies
docs.text:
Two hierarchies describe where an SDL executes and what it executes (Fig. 8A).

Equipment hierarchy (where):

  • Laboratory: the complete cell.
  • Unit: a group of devices that together perform one process step.
  • Device: the smallest piece of equipment the software can command on its own.

The cell in Figure 1 has four units:

  • a dispensing unit (gantry, dispensers and balance);
  • a transfer unit (SCARA and articulated arm);
  • a mixing unit;
  • a characterization unit.

Execution hierarchy (what):

  • Experiment: preparing and characterizing a set of formulations.
  • Workflow: device operations ordered by their dependencies, possibly spanning several units.
  • Device operation: a single command to one device, such as dosing powder once.

Orchestration systems use their own names for groupings between these levels (task, protocol, sequence, campaign). The review uses the neutral terms above so the systems can be compared.

docs.title: Four functional layers
docs.text:
The functions of orchestration software fall into four layers (Fig. 8B):

Layer Role L4 · Decision making Chooses experimental conditions and requests workflows. It may be a person, an external program or AI agent, or a planner built into the software. L3 · Workflow orchestration Orders device operations, allocates devices, and pauses or retries execution. L2 · Device integration Delivers operations to devices and returns their results and errors. L1 · Device control Drives motors and reads sensors in firmware or vendor software. This layer sits outside the orchestrator.

Five common functions cut across the layers:

  • resource and location management;
  • data and traceability;
  • error handling;
  • human-in-the-loop support;
  • external integration.

Resource and location management matters most for formulation, because tool changes, container transfers and material consumption change the state of the cell at every step.

docs.title: Interfaces to devices and decision makers
docs.text: Orchestration software meets the laboratory through two interfaces.

docs.title: Device interface (L2 ↔ L1)
docs.text:
Laboratory standards describe device capabilities in a common format across manufacturers:

  • SiLA 2 defines typed device features with discovery, progress notifications and status subscriptions [167].
  • OPC UA LADS builds information models for laboratory and analytical devices on industrial OPC UA [168].
  • ROS 2 plays the same role for robots [96].

Devices without such support are driven through vendor SDKs, APIs, or serial and TCP commands wrapped in device adapters. Examples:

  • the Opentrons Python Protocol API drives Opentrons liquid handlers [15];
  • PyLabRobot exposes Hamilton, Tecan and Opentrons platforms through one interface [88];
  • Hamilton STAR systems are programmed through the vendor's VENUS environment.

Among the eight open-source systems:

  • EOS and ARES OS call SiLA 2 devices directly.
  • MADSci mainly uses REST nodes.
  • UniLabOS offers ROS 2 as an option.
  • NIMO registers devices as MCP servers.

Data standards such as AnIML and Allotrope define how results are stored, not how devices are controlled [169], [170].

docs.title: External control interface (L4 ↔ L3)
docs.text:
This interface connects decision makers to the orchestrator. It can take the form of graphical interfaces, REST or gRPC APIs, Python clients and, increasingly, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for AI agents [171]. All eight systems expose HTTP or gRPC APIs, and EOS, UniLabOS and NIMO also support MCP. An agent connected through MCP may itself act as L4, or it may call a planner inside the software. MCP support alone therefore does not determine where decisions are made.

Data flows both ways through these interfaces. Validated measurements stream to models, and decisions come back as executable workflows. Real-time dashboards let researchers watch balances, mixers and characterizers, see what the planner proposed and step in when a value drifts.

The digital twin sits behind the same interface and rehearses each requested workflow before L3 releases it to the devices. What remains is deciding which workflows to request: see Data & Decision Models and LLMs & AI Agents.

docs.title: Open-Source Orchestration Software
docs.text:
Step 6 · Orchestrate

This page summarizes Section 7.2 of the review and reproduces Supplementary Table S1, which details Figure 8C. The layer terms (L1–L4) are defined in System Architecture & Orchestration.

docs.title: Scope and selection
docs.text:
Software for integrating laboratory devices is being developed worldwide, but not all of it orchestrates physical experiments:

  • FireWorks and AiiDA manage computational workflows and provenance [153], [154].
  • XDL describes chemical procedures [155].
  • FINALES brokers requests between laboratories [156].
  • Bluesky coordinates measurement sequences at large facilities [157].

The review compared systems that meet five criteria:

  1. They integrate and control physical devices.
  2. They are intended for general use.
  3. They have an open-source core.
  4. They were updated within the 12 months before November 2026.
  5. They are documented in a publication or official documentation.

Eight systems qualified: MADSci [158], AlabOS [159], EOS [160], HELAO-async [161], IvoryOS [162], UniLabOS [163], NIMO [164] and ARES OS [165].

Two notable systems were excluded:

  • ChemOS [143] pioneered orchestration for SDLs, but its successor ChemOS 2.0 [144] is a configuration that accompanies a publication rather than a general package.
  • OCTOPUS [166] publishes no license.

Each function was rated as provided through standard mechanisms (configuration files and documented formats and APIs), partially provided, or not provided. Ratings are based on the code and documentation of the repository versions listed below.

docs.title: What they share and where they differ
docs.text:
All eight systems accept execution requests, manage step order, register and issue device operations and return their results. All record runs and results and expose external APIs. They differ in four respects:

  1. Branching and scheduling.
    • Result-dependent branching is standard in AlabOS, EOS, HELAO-async, IvoryOS and ARES OS.
    • Choosing an executable step among concurrent workflows is standard in MADSci, AlabOS, EOS and UniLabOS. NIMO and ARES OS run one procedure at a time.
  2. Built-in planning. EOS, IvoryOS and NIMO offer built-in selection of the next conditions.
  3. Resource modeling, the sharpest divide.
    • Only MADSci and UniLabOS track tool mounting and container locations as parent–child relations, and remaining material as quantities.
    • AlabOS and EOS reserve devices and locations across steps.
  4. Alerts. Only MADSci, AlabOS and HELAO-async alert people through external channels such as email.

Choosing a system

No system provides every function. Choosing one means working out which functions your workflows need as standard and which can be added through extension points. In formulation, tool, container and material states change at every step, so built-in resource and location management reduces custom state-tracking code. The review did not compare implementation effort or run-time performance.
